speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-3, an Act relating to cash contributions by Canada in respect of insured health services provided under provincial health care insurance plans and amounts payable by Canada in respect of extended health care services and to amend and repeal certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, at the point at which I was interrupted last week, I was beginning to say what I thought was significant about the Canada Health Act in terms of the history of medicare. I was saying why we feel it is important to support the Bill, regardless of its many flaws and the many things it does not do. The main reason for this, and this was said well by one particular witness, Dr. Robert Evans, is that this national consensus against extra billing and user fees has the possibility of finally putting behind us the debate about extra billing and user fees.
Something I have regretted for the last four years as health critic for my Party is that so much time had to be spent on the subject of extra billing and user fees when there are many other questions which have to be faced with regard to the future of our health care system. These two issues, extra billing and user fees, have dominated the political debate vis-a-vis medicare, and rightfully so. 1 am not complaining about that. 1 am saying that we are now at a point where hopefully we can go beyond arguing about extra billing and user fees and accept that these are practices which are regarded as unacceptable by all three political Parties. We should begin to face some of the other questions that remain as far as the future of our health care system is concerned.
1 acknowledge that this issue has existed since the beginning of medicare. The question of whether or not extra billing and user fees were or were not anomalies or violations of the spirit of medicare is an issue which has been ambivalent since the beginning of medicare. Now when we come so near to the end
of the debate on the Canada Health Act, we are saying that that ambivalence and ambiguity are finally resolved and we as the Parliament of Canada declare that extra billing and user fees are violations of the principle of medicare and that, as far as we are concerned, the debate on that issue is over.
I call on the provinces, particularly those provinces which have indicated opposition to the Canada Health Act, to respect the decision of Parliament and seek ways of eliminating extra billing and user fees in the provinces where these practices exist, and not to seek ways of getting around the Canada Health Act or making political hay out of whatever the provinces will argue will be the result of the Canada Health Act. It is important as well, not just federally but provincially, to go beyond the debate about extra billing and user fees and turn to some of the other questions.
There are two other things about this Bill which I think are important. Both of them are in the nature of what I would call conceptual victories or breakthroughs. These breakthroughs will not have any impact the day after the Act is passed but are important in the sense of reshaping our view of the health care system. The first one deals with the amendment to Clause 9 which uses the phrase "health care practitioner" and in particular talks about health care practitioners as being a group to which doctors, nurses and other health care practitioners belong. In this way, all of the health care professionals in the health care system are equal. They have different tasks but they are all health care practitioners, and that is the significance of the language in Clause 9 as amended.
Clause 9 as amended reads "other health care practitioners". This is the kind of wording for which the Canadian Nurses Association and others lobbied strenuously. I would like to take this opportunity to say how important a role those associations played in making sure that this kind of amendment was actually achieved. Their members would not stand for anything less and would not be satisfied with any token wording. They wanted it made clear that "health care practitioner" was a concept which, if it were to be included, must include everyone, and that is what they finally got from the Government. I am happy to see that the Government finally came around to that point of view and found a way to include wording such as that which is permissive in nature. It allows the provinces to begin to see the health care system in that way but does not require the provinces to do so. I think that that is a very important conceptual breakthrough in the Canada Health Act.
The second breakthrough has to do with an amendment which we proposed to the preamble to the Act. To the paragraph which indicated how we could expect to achieve further improvements in the well-being of Canadians, we had added

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
the notion of "collective action against the social, environmental and occupational causes of disease". It seems to me that the next big success that we will achieve with respect to health care in the country will not come so much from advanced technology, although that will be important. The next big success we as a society will see will come when we begin to address collectively the social, environmental and occupational causes of disease. That will have the same effect as did the earlier massive success when, in this country at least, we addressed the questions of clean water and sanitary conditions and the various other ways in which we wiped out the threat of infectious disease such as it existed at one time.
I wanted to call that amendment to the attention of the House because I think we have now begun to admit that we need to go beyond the curative physician-dominated system that exists in terms of the health care delivery system, and even beyond the individual, preventive, lifestyle kinds of approaches which are now popular with respect to health care. Those approaches are crucial but they will not do the trick for the millions and millions of Canadians whose health is being threatened by the things that only we as a society can do something about. I think the amendment to the preamble is particularly important in that respect.
Another amendment that I should like to call to the attention of the House and which we were responsible for implementing, is the amendment to Clause 10 which deals with universality. It calls for the provision of all services on uniform terms and conditions. This would go some way toward preventing the development of a multi-tier health care delivery system in provinces which, for instance, collect health care premiums and where there might have been some inclination in the future to stream health care consumers into various forms of health care delivery according to whether they had paid their premiums or were on premium assistance. I believe this was at least being contemplated and probably is still being contemplated in the Province of Ontario. In these circumstances, certain kinds of health care consumers might be streamed into community clinics on the basis of the fact that they are receiving premium assistance or whatever, and others who have paid the premiums would be eligible for fee for service and more individualized service. It is not that we have anything against community health clinics, Mr. Speaker, quite the contrary, but we do not want to see them turn into a form of ghettoization for certain Canadians. We want the concept to be broadened and used effectively for the well-being of all Canadians. That was the intent of the amendment to Clause 10.
We suggested some other amendments which were not accepted. We moved an amendment regarding the setting up of a national health council to provide continuing attention to the future of medicare. We called for stronger penalties because we have our doubts about the effectiveness of the penalties as they now stand. We hope, as I said earlier, however, that the provinces will respond to this national consensus against extra billing and user fees.
We moved an amendment regarding the acceptable ratio of ward beds as against private and semi-private beds. We were concerned that with increasing emphasis on hospitals having to generate more and more of their own revenue, accessibility might be threatened, not through extra billing and user fees but through the availability of beds that could be afforded through the provincial plan and not through extra insurance. That was rejected also.
We moved an amendment regarding parliamentary accountability because we felt that, with respect to other program conditions for which the Act gives the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) discretion, too much discretion was being given to the Minister. We felt that there should have been a way of involving the House of Commons, and particularly the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, in adjudicating whether provinces were actually in violation of the principles of medicare. That was rejected.
We moved an amendment about positive incentives for provinces that move quickly to clean up their act with respect to extra billing and user fees. We felt that the Act as it stands is too punitive in nature and does not include enough positive incentives for provinces that want to act in this respect. That was rejected.
In committee I moved the amendment that was suggested by the Canadian Association of Interns and Residents. That was rejected, although the Government brought forward an amendment which it claims meets those needs. Opposition Parties, however, are not satisfied with that amendment nor are the residents and interns, and only time will tell whether it actually meets the needs.
At this point in the life of medicare, Mr. Speaker, it will take some political will, some imagination, some going beyond the traditional positions that everyone cherishes with regard to his or her own approach to medicare in order to address some of the very difficult questions facing us in the years ahead. We will feel very soon the impact of important demographic trends with respect to the aging of our society. I believe we should be laying the infrastructure, the planning and concepts to deal with that problem now, not wait until it hits us like a two-ton truck. There is a lack of foresight, I believe, on the part of governments which do not want to face up to the need for long-term investment to be able to meet those needs. So we have that demographic problem, Mr. Speaker. We have a technological problem as well. We have more and more lifesaving, diagnostic and therapeutic advanced technology which uses up more and more of the finite source of funds. Unless we can find a way to get unlimited funds, we are going to have some very difficult questions to answer down the road as to the allocation of health care dollars. I am aware that whenever this matter is brought up, particularly by the doctors, there is a great deal of criticism, and justly so in that doctors often bring it up in the wrong context. They often bring it up as a way of trying to win an argument on another point, Mr. Speaker.
April 2, 1984

There are questions having to do with the allocation of health care dollars because there is not an infinite amount of money, and there will be difficult decisions to be made. They may not be made in the way in which the medical community would like, and, as I say, I believe it is often brought up in a misleading way by the medical community. Nevertheless, there are difficult decisions to be made about the allocation of health care resources. Canadians will have to pay more attention to how their health care dollars are being spent. We will have to find a way, as we did through medicare when we found a way to go beyond the allocation of health care resources by the marketplace, and we will have to find a way to go beyond the present system which lays itself open more and more to the charge that bureaucrats are allocating health care resources by political and fiscal imperatives instead of health care imperatives.
The answer is not, Mr. Speaker, as so many in the CMA and others would have us believe, to return to allocation by the marketplace. The answer is to find the political will to go beyond both the marketplace and fiscal and political imperatives and find a third way in which we can face up to those difficult decisions about the allocation of health care dollars. At the same time as we want to go beyond the present system, we must resist the temptation, as we do in so many other areas of our economic and political life, to see, in the inadequacy of the present state of affairs, a reason to go back rather than ahead. I believe that is something, Mr. Speaker, which we should keep in mind.
There will have to be on the part of the federal Government a willingness to reopen the whole question of the funding relationship with the provinces. There must be a willingness to go back to the table and say, "We have all these other problems we have to meet, how can we meet them together?", rather than having the stubborn attitude that, "We provide a certain amount of money through block funding and that is it. We will put conditions on that money"-which I support- "but that is all we are going to do".
1 believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare and future Ministers of National Health and Welfare, will have to be willing to sit down with the provinces and renegotiate that funding relationship so we can have a full-fledged financial partnership with respect to medicare.
There are many other questions we will have to face but I do not have the time to go into them. There will be the question of transportation in northern Ontario, for instance, and other remote parts of the country where people do not, in a sense, have equal access to hospital care. They must spend a lot more money than people living in urban centres to provide their families with the kind of hospital care which may be recommended by their physicians. These are all questions and conditions which impede the realization of the original vision of medicare. There are things which are still on the agenda, Mr. Speaker. Hopefully, with the passage of this Act, we can put the debate about extra billing and user fees behind us and trust that provinces will see the wisdom of this and act in the very
Canada Health Act
near future to eliminate extra billing and user fees so that the spirit in which we in this House approach this Act will be infectious and we will see that kind of co-operative attention paid to our health care system from here on.

Mr. Speaker, I was wondering if the Member would advise the House whether this Bill in any way prevents doctors from practising outside the system? In other words, can they practise outside the provincial medical system and send their bills directly to their patients?
Mr. Speaker, let me repeat the question just to make sure I have it correct. Can doctors opt out, bill their patients and then have their patients bill the plan? Is that what you are saying?
Can doctors opt out?

Doctors can do anything they like so long as they do not extra-bill their patients. That is my view and that of the parliamentary task force, on which my friend and I both sat, of what constitutes extra billing. Extra billing is when patients are charged more than the plan will pay them.

Will the Member advise me where in this Bill a province is prevented from reimbursing a patient for money he may have paid to a doctor? Let us say that a doctor practised medicine in California and the patient saw him there, or an Ontario patient went to Quebec and saw a doctor and paid him directly. Could the patient be reimbursed? If the patient went to the Mayo Clinic in New York, could he be reimbursed? Indeed, could he be reimbursed if he saw a specialist in Ontario and the specialist said he did not practise state medicine, "If you want to collect from the province and the province does not pay you, fine, I do not care. You pay me".
Would the province be prevented from paying that patient something toward the bill?
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Hon. Member understands the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No, that is obvious.

The Bill does not prevent anything. It simply says that if extra billing occurs, there will be a dollar for dollar penalty. I have explained what constitutes extra billing. What the Bill does is to provide for a penalty for extra billing to the extent that it exists in any particular province. How particular provinces decide to regulate, eliminate or control, or whatever they decide to do with extra billing, will be the business of the provinces. I am sure the Hon. Member would not want me to make recommendations on how individual provinces make judgements in the particular cases he brings up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to express my concern at one aspect of the Bill which has not been addressed as it should be. The Hon. Member who has just spoken is an

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
expert in various aspects of the Bill and I would like to hear his opinion.
As he well knows, medical advances are so rapid that it is essential to develop a system of training to give extra attention to these various advances, which will reflect themselves in better care. That aspect has not been addressed in this Bill. We think in terms of quantity, geographical distribution and universality, yet we do not think in terms of quality of care. This requires an extra effort on the part of the graduate physicians and doctors who have spent x-number of years in conventional and in specialized training, often at their own expense. The Bill does not address itself to supporting these people, giving them the extra help they need to get that training and practise it efficiently. Without that category of physician there will be a deterioration of medical services in this country. In the various speeches I have heard the Hon. Member make, I have not heard him address himself to that particular issue.

Mr. Speaker, the nature and quality of the training that physicians receive is not something over which the federal Government has a great deal of say. The Hon. Member is a physician himself and knows that, to a great extent, physicians are a self-regulating monopoly. However, there is a lot of public money spent on them. There is a great investment made by the public in medical schools. I do not have the numbers at hand, but I am sure it is a phenomenal amount of public money which is spent to train physicians. Some of them then turn around, in their own peculiar way of saying how grateful they are, and say that they do not feel they can make enough money here, and so they go to Houston or some place else.
I think great improvements could be made in the quality of care, Mr. Speaker. We must first identify more clearly what we mean by care. Care is not only the precision and insight with which physicians make judgements. Care has to do with how many nurses are on the ward, the conditions in which patients live out their days in hospitals, what kind of services are available in the home, and how humane the total health care system is. We have to consider those areas in addressing quality of care. It seems to me that physicians have some way to go in order to catch up with that view. They must begin to treat a person more as a whole person and less as a case study.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is showing a little bit of ignorance toward what constitutes quality care. First and foremost, a great deal of the training that physicians and surgeons must take is not taken in Canada and is not taken with the help of public funds. That type of training is not available in this country. Most of these people will go offshore or to the United States and will spend years of their time in training. They will do it at considerable personal expense. There is a tendency for breakdowns in their families as a result of being separated from them.
With regard to the quality of care, the humane aspect does not show itself in some of the procedures which are practised.
Time and again the essential part of the treatment is the skill of the physician in acquiring the new techniques and approaches. The follow-up care is in the hands of the rest of the team.
Therefore, there are two factors here. The first is that the quality of care is achieved without financial assistance from the federal Government, at the expense of the individual doctors. Second, in most situations the doctor must be the person in charge who must take the overall responsibility, something which cannot be done by other members of the health care team.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on third reading on Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act, it is important to state at the outset that our contribution to this debate, both at this stage and throughout the study of this Bill, is based on the principle that the Progressive Conservative Party, from the very beginning of the debate on a national health care system, has supported just such a system, namely a national health care system. It is important to remind the House and the Canadian public that this is the case. It dates back to 1956 when at a national convention the Party in fact moved a policy principle in which the Party committed itself to a national health care system to be achieved in co-operation with the provinces. That system was to be one of which Canadians could be proud and which it was within the resources of Canadians to afford. Those principles established by the Party in 1956, Mr. Speaker, are the principles on which this Party stands today. It is from that basis that we complete the debate on the health care system.
It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that it was only a few years after that conclusion of the Party in 1956, during the Government of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, that the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act of 1957 was passed. In 1962, the medicare system came into Saskatchewan. This was done through the co-operation of the Saskatchewan Government of Mr. Tommy Douglas as well as of Prime Minister Diefenbaker. These two gentlemen both gave tribute to the contribution that was made at that time.
I make those statements at the outset, Mr. Speaker, to allay the suggestions made by some people that the Progressive Conservative Party is not in favour of a universal national health care system. The record not only supports that, it substantiates it. Having made those comments, I hope we can go on to real issues rather than continue to address issues which in fact are not issues at all.
Before us we have a Bill which has been largely amended through the committee process. It has seen a number of amendments brought forward by the Government, by our Party, as well as by the New Democratic Party. I believe the Bill before us is more realistic in terms of the health care system than the Bill which we addressed at second reading. When I use the word realistic, that is the sense in which I use it.
The Minister is in the House today. I would like to thank her for the kind comments she made during her participation
April 2, 1984

in third reading. Even the preamble of the Bill was changed after second reading. This remains in front of the national agenda on health care. I will quote in part the amendment to the preamble. It reads:
-that it is not the intention of the government of Canada that any of the powers, rights, privileges or authorities vested in Canada or the provinces under the provisions of the Constitution Act, 1867 (formerly named the British North America Act, 1867), or any amendments thereto, or otherwise, be by reason of this Act abrogated or derogated from or in any way impaired;
That simply means that the Government is concerned that the Bill in part could be seen to be moving into or at least affecting the constitutional jurisdiction of the health field which is within provincial rights. I do not have the right to speak for the provinces. I do not know if the provinces will take this Bill or provisions of this Bill to the courts. It is important to note in the House today that that amendment was brought in by the Government, I suggest, because of the Government's own concern and fear that parts of this Bill could be seen by the courts to be involving the federal Government in provincial jurisdictions. The reason I raise this matter is that it is at the very heart and nub of what I believe the health care system should be. It should be a system based on co-operation and recognition that the provinces have the primary responsibility for health care delivery systems. It should be based on the recognition that the federal Government has a responsibility to maintain that the five principles of medicare which we support are not only kept intact but that the system does not violate them in any way. As we look at the action of the provinces, it will be very interesting to see whether or not Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act, will be challenged in court.
What is of greater significance is the amendments to Clause 3 and Clause 4. Clause 3 is entitled "Canada Health Care Policy" and there were substantial sections of Clause 3 removed by the Government through amendment. In fact, the words that it removed were, "It is hereby declared that the Canadian health care policy should be designed and administered: (a) to encourage effective allocation of the nation's health resources: (b), to facilitate the provision of adequate health services throughout Canada".
Surely no one could quarrel with the statement that the health care system should facilitate the provision of adequate health services throughout Canada. One must raise the question as to why the federal Government feels it necessary to remove those words from the Bill which is called the Canada Health Act. 1 think the answer is quite straightforward. I stated earlier that although the Bill does not address the Canada health system as I would have liked it to, I believe that the amendment that the Government then moved is more significant and makes the Bill more realistic because Clause 3 states that:
-the primary objective of Canadian health care policy is to protect, promote and restore the physical and mental well-being of residents of Canada and to facilitate reasonable access to health services without financial or other barriers.
Let us go to Clause 4, which describes the purpose of the Bill. It reads:
______________________________________2607
Canada Health Act
The purpose of this Act is to establish criteria and conditions that must be met before full payment may be made under the Act of 1977-
Those words are significant in the sense that the Minister had to recognize, through the amendment procedure, that what the Canada Health Act was really addressing was not so much the future of health care as what she was going to put forward in the Act, that is, financial penalties for extra billing and user fees. The national agenda should have been to consider the question of what we see in national health care services in the future; what those services should be; what model should best be brought into being through co-operation with the provinces while keeping in mind the provinces' primary responsibility; and finally addressing the question, difficult though it may be, of how we allocate resources both human and financial to meet the health care system of the future.
I suggest that, unfortunately, the opportunity to do that was greatly restricted by the scope of the Bill and, in fact, the amendments restricted the Bill even further. Members present in the House today who sat on the committee would agree with me, I believe, that there was hardly an exception to the fact that as witnesses appeared before the committee they would address the matter of extra billing and user fees and then go on to say what they thought should be the national agenda. The national agenda was: What do we do about an aging population; what do we do about technology; what do we do about preventive health care; what do we do about co-operation with the provinces, and what do we do about resources. Those are the issues with which the House must deal. Unfortunately, this Bill does not do so.
Having said that, while amendments which we brought forward were rejected by the Government in many cases, the principle of our amendment was accepted by the Government in other amendments. I mention only a few to make the point. One concerns the health care practitioner. I want to point out that the concept of the health care practitioner is now part of the Canada Health Act in Clause 9 and the definition clause. I also want to state very clearly to the public and the provinces that this does not impose an extra financial burden on the provinces. I suggest that it is no different from Section 4(3) of the Medical Care Act of 1966 in which, for example, there were services not covered through the insured services, such as optometrical services, which the province could in fact provide in part through an insured service with the province only. They were never covered through the federal-provincial financial transfer system.
Since we have flagged that the health care system is a system consisting totally of health care practitioners, it is important to note that the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Nurses' Association and other professionals who are familiar with the health care system realize that we must move toward a more holistic approach both to medicine and to the health care professional. When talking about a holistic system, we must consciously put forward the fact that the health care system should address the other concepts of preventive health care. While I believe it will always have illness as its primary

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
orientation, since the health care system obviously must address illness, it should not be restricted only to the concept of addressing illness.
I believe that the amendment respecting the health care practitioner does give the provinces and health care practitioners an opportunity to take an approach to health care resources, that is professionals, finances and the philosophy of holistic medicine, without imposition on the provinces themselves.
I am sure that members of the committee and the House would agree that in terms of the Canadian Medical Association and amendments to Clause 12(2), I have spoken on it as much possibly as anyone. I should point out that the wording in that clause in the original draft Bill was that medical professionals had the right to reasonable compensation. What does reasonable compensation mean and how does one approach the question of reasonable compensation? I go back to Mr. Justice Emmet Hall who said in his report in 1980 that the health care system in fact could be eroded in the future if extra billing and user fees were allowed to continue or to expand. However, he never made those statements in isolation. He always added that if that were to take place through legislation there had to be a system whereby medical professionals would be entitled to reasonable compensation. Those two views were always tied together.
Those were his words in his report, and he reiterated the statement at the committee hearing of February 14, as can be found on page 510. He said, "Accepting that physicians have a right to be fairly and adequately compensated can be stated this way; no more, no less, and the state has a right to be concerned with the problem." I agree with the principles he stated, that there must be fairness and there must be a balance between recognizing professional independence and recognizing the fact that the public which finances the system has the right to services for which they have paid. There must aiso be recognition of the fact that the health care professional not only feels that he or she has been adequately compensated financially but also that psychologically and professionally society recognizes their contribution and their role.
Mr. Justice Hall goes even further in a press article, which appeared as recently as today, in which he states very clearly that medical doctors cannot dictate fees because, in a sense, as we get a national health system they give up in part a certain freedom in exchange for a health care system. But that is the dilemma and the conundrum.
I say to the provinces that the amendment which we brought forward is not binding on the provinces but it is at least a model, or they can now develop models whereby fee structures and fee disputes can be resolved. It is not my purpose, nor is it my right, to dictate to the provinces how this should be done. I simply put forward the principles once again. If the system is to work and if the people within it are to feel that they are making a valid contribution which is recognized by society, I commend that amendment to the provinces for further study.
The toughest question in health care is the question of cost containment. How do we address that question? It is clear that we have to state again that it is not within federal jurisdiction to address this question in isolation. I want to say to all Members of the House and to the Canadian public that when we talk about cost containment, we are not talking in the sense that we want to erode in any way the principles of medicare. It is for the reason that we want to preserve medicare that we must address the question of cost containment.
Let us take a look at the last two years. If one takes a look at the recession, one finds that the Gross National Product used for health care has risen dramatically. If one takes a look at the national deficit, 25 cents of every dollar collected from the taxpayers of Canada is used to service the debt. If we add that 25 cents of every dollar to service the debt, and if we take a look at our safety nets of health care insurance and unemployment insurance, systems which we want to maintain, the real question becomes: when will we get our economic house in order so that the systems and services Canadians want to have maintained can be paid for? That is the issue.
I would like to give a very practical example. I know the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) will make the case more strongly on the economic side, but if we were able to reduce the 25 cents by 5 cents to 20 cents for the servicing of the national debt, it would give us roughly $7 billion to $8 billion. The expenditures of the federal Government in terms of national health care are between $9 billion and $10 billion.
Every time you get up you ask the Government to spend more.

We are getting the traditional catcalls from the Liberals. When a person wants to address these questions, he has to address them, no matter what catcalls he gets and no matter what the difficulty. Additionally, we have to look at the cost of technology and demography. How do we do this? That is the question. I will put it to the House very bluntly and in a very straightforward way. We cannot do it in the federal House by imposition. The only way to do it, when we talk about a health care system which is a national plan and in which the provinces have primary responsibility, is to sit down with the provinces and look at the issues.
If there has been anything lacking over the last few years in the health care system, it has been co-operation. We have to return to co-operative federalism because we cannot impose from here, nor will we have a better system because we impose. The best way to do it is to get back to economic principles and increase economic activity. If we look at the statistics, as the economic recession deepened we got into more and more difficulty in the health care system. Surely the global answer is once again to establish an economic climate where people who are risk takers are able to invest and feel that their investment and their return will be seen as their right to invest in the economy. We must not look at the question from a reductions point of view. We cannot take an
April 2, 1984

ever increasing piece of the pie from the general paying public, but we should increase the size of the economic activity of Canada.
Those are very difficult issues. I would like to give another example. National voluntary agencies want to become involved in the health care system. Let us get them involved. Let us get them around the table to see how it can be done. I am referring to agencies such as the Victorian Order of Nurses. There are many suggestions one could make in this field, but my greatest suggestion would be to get on with some of the positive aspects rather than always to raise the question of how we do it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member, my official critic in the Official Opposition, a question concerning the alleged underfunding of the system. I am sure the Hon. Member will excuse me if I do not have the details, but the figures are well known to all of us who worked on medicare in committee. In the years which followed block funding, years in which the federal funding went up to a national average of 58 per cent of the so-called medicare, extra billing and user fees started to grow instead of remaining at a low level as they had done for years, and thus the crisis we are in was created. How does he reconcile the fact that when we gave the most money extra charges were placed upon the patients? I do not understand his reasoning.

Mr. Speaker, this debate has been going on for some time. If the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) goes back to the previous Budgets of her Government, she will note very clearly that in those Budget statements the Minister of Finance said that through reductions of the EPF the Government over the next period of the EPF would reduce its funding by $5.7 billion, that is $5.7 billion over what had been projected. If she goes to the last Budget, she will see that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said that through the rejigging of the system or because the inflation rate was lower, he found an additional amount of money. Then it came out that it was not only $269 million; there was an additional sum of money, in the area of $700 million, which was part of the system.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What does that have to do with my question?

1 will get to your question. When we look at block funding, what the Minister had said for so long, which was rejected, was that the provinces were diverting money that they were receiving either for health care or for post-secondary education. They were diverting it into other fields of provincial responsibility. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall very clearly stated that there was no evidence to that effect at all.
If one takes a look at the manner in which health care systems developed in the 1960s and onward, for example, one finds that the average inflation rate during that decade was approximately 4.5 per cent, but health care costs were rising at an average of 12.2 per cent. That built-in cost is now within the system. Additionally, there have been without any question other factors which have added to the cost of the health care
Canada Health Act
system well beyond any escalation of cost sharing from the federal Government or, as we now call it, block funding.
The question the Minister has to relate more directly is, what percentage of their provincial budgets the provinces are now expending for health care as against previous years? If we take a province such as Alberta, it pays more to date per capita for health care than any other province. If we take a look at provinces in Atlantic Canada, over 50 per cent of their total provincial budget is now transfer payments. The point I am making to the Minister is that in each case those provinces are spending between 25 cents and 30 cents of their total budget on health care, and that is rising. The ability to afford more is the serious question which those provinces and we in the House have to address.

Mr. Speaker, I join late in the debate on this Bill. Unfortunately, it was not possible for me to participate on second reading or in committee. I regret that. However, I believe that the committee did a first-class job. This Bill by and large fulfills the requirements that the parliamentary task force on fiscal arrangements set out with respect to the medicare and health care system and the federal Government's responsibility in that system.
You, Mr. Speaker, will personally remember being a part of that task force and our considerations on the various criteria,
in which the federal Government participated, in health care programs in Canada. I refer again to Clause 7 of the Bill where the five criteria of public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability and accessability are set out. A number of people have suggested that it is not the federal obligation to look after and ensure that there are these criteria, but I asked my constituents that question. I asked: "Do you believe that the federal Government has an obligation to ensure the existence of a national medicare and hospitalization system and insist on specific national standards, and does it have the right to penalize provinces that do not comply with national standards?" My constituents answered 72 per cent yes and 21 per cent no. Despite what Colin Brown has indicated in the large advertisements of the National Citizens' Coalition, the Act has a good deal of public support. This Party supports this Bill.
It is very important that matters such as user fees be banned. In the task force we studied the question of user fees and how hospitals, in order to discourage people from using their facilities, charged a fee. That fee either had to be so large as to be punitive and therefore hurt the poor and the sick, or be so small as to be negligible and, therefore, a fee that would not deter anybody, and one that would be used up in administration. When we were in Whitehorse, we found that the hospitals, under the auspices of this Minister, were directed to have a user fee for emergency services. The study of that user fee indicated that the entire fee was used up in the administration of trying to collect it. That was a rather foolish type of fee which, thank goodness, no longer exists. This Bill bans that class of fee.
A great deal has been said with respect to extra billing. In our tours of the country, we found certain situations in certain provinces, particularly in Saskatchewan which at that time was under a New Democratic government. That province not only allowed its doctors to collect from the medicare system, but to charge extra to the patients. The doctor had it both ways. He could bill the system and bill the patient. That was an extra type of fee. The same situation existed in a number of the maritime provinces. That kind of billing is improper. To rely on the system, to look after all your credit headaches, all of your problems, and then charge the patient an extra $2, $5 or $10, whatever the patient can afford, is to set up a double system of medical care.
I referred earlier to the activities of the National Citizens' Coalition, which had the temerity to ask, "How would you like your open-heart surgery done by a civil servant?", or, "How would you like your baby delivered by someone who delivers the mail?" It suggested that this Act would somehow destroy the ability of persons to see a doctor. I say, nonsense, Sir.
Earlier on in today's debate, I asked if this Bill in any way required that a doctor sign up or be committed to the medicare system. In fact, it does not. Nowhere in this Bill does it say that a medical practitioner must practise within the provincial medical system. He is entitled, if he can qualify, to practise
April 2, 1984

any way he wants and to practice within the hospital system in the way he already practises. He is entitled to send his bills to his patient in the normal course of events. He is not recruited, conscripted or forced to belong to the Ontario system, the Manitoba system or any other system.
Having said that, Sir, there is nothing within this Bill that in any way prevents the provinces from reimbursing to the level of the medicare fees in that province the patients who go to see doctors who do not belong to the system. Nothing in this Bill prevents that from happening. It may be said by some that that is a form of extra billing, but how in the world can it be extra billing if the doctors do not even belong to the system? How can a doctor extra-bill the system if he is not even part of the system, any more than a doctor who works at the Mayo Clinic or a doctor who practises in Florida or a doctor who practises in another province is part of the system? Indeed, as far as the other provinces are concerned and as far as doctors practising out of the jurisdiction are concerned, the concept of universality and portability contemplates the reimbursement of fees paid out by patients to doctors by the provincial system.
Doctors who do not belong to the system do not bill the system. Therefore, their bills can in no way be treated as extra billing. That billing is not extra to anything if the doctor is not part of that system. The real political question is whether or not this Minister would try to say that if a province reimburses a patient for seeing a doctor who does not belong to a system, that province was in some way evading the provisions of the Canada Health Act.
Before I discuss that, Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss a question which I put to my own constituents. I will read into the record the question I put to my constituents. The question was: "About 14 per cent of Ontario doctors are opted out of medicare. These doctors bill their patients directly. Do you believe that patients of opted-out doctors should be able to collect from the provincial Government that portion of the fee billed to them by their doctor that would normally be paid directly to the doctor if the doctor had not opted out?"
In answer to that question, 67 per cent of my constituents said yes and 26 per cent said no. I suggest to the Minister and to any provincial Minister who might be involved that they might have a very difficult time saying to someone who went to the Mayo Clinic or to a specialist who was not interested in medicare that he could not be reimbursed for his expenses. Any government which indicated that would be in serious trouble indeed.
However, the Act does go a long way toward making sure that universality exists. The provisions of the Act specifically indicate that the service must be comprehensive. That means that people should be able to find medical service that is in accordance with a provincial universal system anywhere in the province. To that extent, if a province would not operate on the basis of having medical service generally available, then, in my view, it would be in default of its conditions. It would not be in default by opting out or by imposing extra billing but by not making sure that there were medical practitioners generally
Canada Health Act
able to offer services to those who are entitled to rely on medical service without the payment of an extra bill.
In that sense, Sir, I think the committee did an excellent job by introducing the concept of reasonable compensation through the amendments which require a type of arbitration to determine the fair fees medical practitioners should charge for their work. The arbitration of fees as conceived by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall is a kind of arbitration that protects not only the practitioner but also protects the public. I think that the committee, in introducing that concept of arbitration, has provided a worthwhile service to medicare.
One of the major concerns we all have is about the rising cost of health care. That cost is rising because of a number of factors. The first factor is the enormous amount of new technology that is coming on stream. The Minister has indicated that she pays for 50 per cent of the medicare system, but does she pay for 50 per cent of the health care system in the broad sense? The answer is no. In the Province of Ontario she pays for perhaps 38 per cent or 40 per cent of the health care system.
A good part of the payments for the health care system are for technology and for making people healthier in non-traditional ways. This is part of the health care technology that exists, and as that technology carries on and as people, because of that technology, live longer, the cost of health care will rise dramatically. We must come to grips, either federally, provincially or as a nation, with the cost of health care. Obviously, if we carry on as we do, we could well reach the point where health care takes a far greater percentage of our income and our national productivity than might be appropriate for a growing country.
One of the suggestions I received to deal with that issue was to take a look at some of the tort liability concerns of doctors. The Minister will know that following what has happened in the United States, medical practitioners are gravely concerned about being sued for malpractice. Often lawsuits are brought even though the doctor has probably done almost everything conceivably possible required to do a first-class job. Whether it was a first-class effort or not, it can be seen in a considerably different way in hindsight than it was seen in foresight.
Second, we must deal with the whole question of the tort liability of a doctor for negligence. I hope that the Minister will do something in terms of negotiations with her provincial counterparts. Perhaps she could have the provinces pass some sort of legislation that would restrict the liability of doctors to cases in which there is absolute gross negligence. This is the kind of step that might seriously reduce some of the costs of the health care system. When doctors pay enormous fees for medical malpractice insurance, those fees must be passed on as one of their costs of doing business. It must obviously be passed on somewhere in their fee structure.
Third, the payment system itself under medicare tends to encourage medical practitioners to perform more services than they might otherwise perform if the medicare system were different. There is a fee for attendance at a doctor's office and that fee is minimal. However, patients seem to have the feeling

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
that doctors are cramming in more people per hour in order to receive a reasonable hourly return. The same thing applies with respect to extra tests and procedures. Doctors tell me I can be sued if I do not take all the tests they order. There seems to be a feeling that the present payment system militates in favour of more services and therefore more fees-the more services rendered, the more fees collected and the higher the doctor's income.
A constituent suggested to me that provincial governments could reward people who did not see their doctor. At the present time, in the course of a year most of us see a doctor. If a rebate or some sort of benefit were paid for not using the system or only using it in a minimal way, the number of usages could be cut down. Perhaps there could be a tax rebate or a medical fees rebate or, in Ontario, an Ontario hospital insurance premium rebate or even a rebate to those who do not pay premiums. The Minister knows that there has been an enormous explosion in the use of the system and that that has created overcrowding in hospitals and in doctors' offices. It is part of the cost we face in making medical services more or less free.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to address the question of portability. One thing has been omitted from the Bill that I had hoped to find there, and that is, some type of clearing system organized by the federal Government for the payment of interprovincial medical charges. For instance, if I go to British Columbia and need to see a doctor or go to a hospital, there is the possibility that I might not pay or that the Ontario Government might not pay or that the Ontario Government would only pay an Ontario fee, which is not necessarily a British Columbia fee. The system should provide that a doctor in British Columbia would bill a central system and be reimbursed directly. The central system would then collect from the province. This problem was mentioned to us by doctors when we were on tour. I hope that the Minister will be able to work out a type of central clearing system for interprovincial billings for medical and hospital services with provincial Health Ministers. Doctors or hospitals who render service to a tourist should not feel that they may not be paid, and that has been the perception in the past.
On balance, we believe that this is a very good Bill and we are prepared to support it. We believe that efforts by the National Citizens' Coalition to castigate the Bill are wrong. If people read the Bill and understand it, they will appreciate that it is an attempt by the Government to come to grips with the concept of universal health care. That is not an easy concept and it will have to be worked on. Anything that is perceived as being free is abused, as we all know very well, but surely this Bill will not result in my gall-bladder being removed by a bureaucrat.

Mr. Speaker, when I first heard the Hon. Member talking about his support for universality in the Bill, I thought that after he had taken a survey of his constituents he had also taken a trip to Damascus. As I listened, however, I discovered that he stopped in Beirut and was shell-shocked.
I have a couple of questions for the Minister. His colleague, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) has indicated that his view of medicare is that it is constitutionally a provincial responsibility and that the provinces should be able to build whatever hospitals they want wherever they want them and provide whatever services they want and that automatically the federal Government should pay 50 per cent of the cost. I should like to know whether that is the Hon. Member's view as well.
The Hon. Member commented about doctors making unnecessary tests. I should like to ask him who should decide which tests a doctor should order. Does he suggest that some citizens are entitled only to second or third class medical care? Who is going to make that decision? Will it be the doctor or some bureaucrat, as he said?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly hope it is not the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) who makes the decision about who gets second-class treatment. I am sure we would all get second-class treatment according to his analysis.
The Hon. Member knows that the provinces are jurisdictionally responsible for the delivery of health care. He knows that as part of the Established Programs Financing Act, going back for many, many years, the federal Government has spent money, originally up to 50 per cent, on the cost of supporting certain services.
The Hon. Member knows that the present Bill provides for a formula for paying block funds to provinces. He knows that, in the broad sense of health care, it is not 50 per cent, but that when we impose conditions we may have to look at the extent of that funding. I suggest that the Hon. Member ought to be hearing from his own constituents. If more conditions are imposed on the Province of New Brunswick than they presently have, then New Brunswick is probably going to need more funding in order to meet those conditions.
I do not know very much about Damascus and I do not know very much about Beirut, and I certainly do not know what they have to do with medicare. Surely the Hon. Member is not suggesting that it is Liberal policy that the Liberal Government will step in and run every hospital and clinic in the country.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by commending the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) for making the remarks he did about the inadequate, to say the least, nature of the arguments put forward recently by the National Citizens' Coalition. I think that criticism of their views by the Hon. Member will have more credibility with that group than any criticisms I might make as a New Democrat. I commend him for having set the record straight for all those who are in the habit of giving the views of the National Citizens' Coalition more credibility than I am. The Act does not do what they claim it does.
April 2, 1984

The Hon. Member mentioned the fact that extra billing has existed in Saskatchewan from the very beginning. That is true, Mr. Speaker. I would ask him to recall, however, that the provision for extra billing was worked out in the middle of one of the hottest political debates that Canada has ever seen-it happened in the middle of a strike by doctors in Saskatchewan.
The government of the day did not do it willingly or because it believed in extra billing; it is something that was worked out in the heat of the moment. It is too often used in a spurious political way to suggest that even New Democrats, or at that time the CCF, are in favour of extra billing. They are not and I should like the Hon. Member to set the record straight.
1 am glad to see that the Hon. Member is consistent on other matters. He was a member of the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements which made a lot of the recommendations which appeared in the Canada Health Act. I think that is one of the reasons why he can speak so favourably about the Bill. It is one of the few instances in this place when recommendations have actually appeared in legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the argument is that the Government of Saskatchewan allowed extra billing because it was in the middle of a strike and in the heat of the moment. I did not know that Members of the New Democratic Party or the CCF settled their principles that easily, gave away their principles that easily, but they certainly remained in that fashion in Saskatchewan because it made sense to them in that province, that is why. It made sense because they knew that if they did not allow some way in which those specialists with extra skills could get something more for their extra skills, they would have problems in their system. Therefore, they went for this extra billing system. I believe their system was wrong. The Ontario system makes a doctor who decides not to belong to the system opt out completely and take the total credit risk for all his patients. He does not know whether his patients will pay him or not but he cannot bill mother province, if he opts out, for any patient. He opts out for all. That makes, in my view, much more economic sense, and I was surprised that Saskatchewan did not go for that. It went for the system of just letting people charge extra on top of what is already a good fee paid to the doctor by the province.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through you I would like to raise two issues with the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). One issue has to do with his concept of opting out. There is one province, the Province of Quebec, which will not allow a physician to opt out and collect money from the insurance plan. A non-participating physician in that province expects to receive full pay from the patient without being reimbursed in any way. Second, inasmuch as the Hon. Member is a member of the legal profession, I wonder what his thoughts are of the concept which was brought forward by one of his judicial experts. That instead of having malpractice insurance, which is a growth industry among lawyers, there would be a system of medical injury compensation in which a
Canada Health Act
central board would adjudicate as to whether or not there actually was malpractice and definite damage to the individual.
Malpractice insurance, as the Hon. Member pointed out, is a very serious problem. The costs of it have been escalating dramatically. Currently, there are three risk groups: neurosurgeons, orthopaedic surgeons and obstetricians and gynaecologists, and they are now paying $2,000 a year. In the next two or three years it is expected to be as much as $5,000 a year. That matter must be considered and I would like to hear the Hon. Member's thoughts on the credibility and the suitable utilization of a system somewhat similar to a compensation board.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I do not feel competent to comment on the Quebec system. There are many other sociological differences between the Province of Quebec and the Province of Ontario, and to comment on how doctors operate in Quebec would perhaps be unfair. I might have my thoughts on it, and the Hon. Member, perhaps, has some thoughts on it as well.
With respect to medical injury compensation, I believe it is a bad move. I believe that what we ought to encourage provinces to do is to restrict the tort liability to gross negligence. I feel that when a person goes to a doctor and has an operation, if there is a mistake in that operation, well, that is the way it is. Unless one can prove the doctor is absolutely grossly negligent, there should be no liability. The same applies when you see a doctor on a consultative basis. Surely to goodness you cannot judge these things after the event. If one wants to go into a compensation scheme, one is going to find that the malpractice insurance was cheap because the news cost will involve a whole series of bureaucrats, a great big office, some type of a board system. All one has to do is to look at what it costs employers today in our Province of Ontario to pay workmens' compensation. The medical malpractice insurance is cheap compared to that.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak in this debate in, I suppose, a kind of mixed mood. For two years I was responsible as the spokesperson for the Conservative Party on the issue of health care. I travelled the country and attended committee meetings and over the two years I learned a great deal which I had not previously known about the health care system in this country. One of the first things 1 learned, Mr. Speaker, is that in some sense we have never had a health care system in the country. In reality, we have 12 different systems, one in each of the ten provinces, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
Something which bothered me about the thought pattern of the Minister, as I listened to her in the House of Commons and in committee, is what I believe to be a fairly deeply held conviction on the Minister's part that there should be a single health care system in the country. I find that bothersome, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
Speaker, perhaps because of my scientific background. It seems to me that when you have a single system for something as important as health, you increase the likelihood of making major mistakes. If everyone is going to be treated in the same way, then you must pick the way to treat them. If you pick the wrong way, Mr. Speaker, the mistake can be a real beaut. When you have 12 systems, perhaps dedicated to similar principles and going at problems in slightly different ways, you have in reality an opportunity system. In an opportunity system, you can learn from each other. In that kind of diversity, Mr. Speaker, I believe that over time you will find more wisdom. You are free to use your best judgement about something. Someone else's judgement from time to time may be better than your own and you can learn from that and build a stronger system.
Today we are debating something called the Canada Health Act. I really feel that a patient out there, an ordinary Canadian, would be hard pressed to read this piece of legislation and come to the conclusion in any sensible way that it is going to do a great deal for the health of Canadians. In reality it is misnamed. It is a health financing act. It is something which could have come from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and been defended in the House from that quarter. Perhaps that is the part which makes me feel the saddest, because we are really not dealing in this Act with the health care system problems of this country. Will any patient in this country be better off the day after this Act is proclaimed? Will their treatment be any better? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the answer is no. Does the Act guarantee better treatment for our patients in the future? Does it make a major contribution to better health care for patients in the future? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we would be hard pressed to find in this piece of legislation that kind of direction and change. Why is that, Mr. Speaker? Patients care about health care. It has been my experience that health care professionals care about health care. I believe that provincial politicians care about health care. Hospital boards and federal politicians care. Everyone in the system cares. They would like to work together, I believe, to produce a better system in the longer term.
We are not dealing today with comprehensive legislation which has been dedicated to the improvement of health care in Canada, and I believe the blame for that must lie with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). It is owing to her personal inability to work co-operatively with the players in the system. This legislation, dealing essentially with provincial jurisdiction, has not been agreed to by the provincial governments, the major players in the system. I believe this legislation was conceived, developed and brought forward to this Chamber primarily to assist the Liberal Party of Canada in gathering the votes of Canadians. That was its motivation, Mr. Speaker.
We all know that out of motivation which we might consider less than adequate we sometimes get good things. There is some good in this legislation because there has been a great deal of fear created in the minds not only of senior citizens
particularly, but of low income people generally, that they were going to be denied access to the health care system because of financial charges of one kind or another. However, I believe the Minister, in part, deliberately created that fear. Now we have legislation which should reduce that fear. If we as Members of this Chamber create a problem, then we have the responsibility to take whatever action we can to reduce the problem.
Earlier this day, Mr. Speaker, we heard about increased costs of the health care system. I have just come from a weekend convention in a province where there is a great deal of concern about that and a sense of bewilderment about where those increased costs are coming from. Each of us who studies the issue can find reasons.
I can remember standing in this House in 1980 and 1981 and asking questions of Ministers along the following lines. It is pretty well a demonstrated fact that for every 1 per cent increase in unemployment you get about a 5 per cent increase in stress related diseases. That manifests itself in the form of wife battering, alcoholism, heart attacks and so on. Through this Government's policies we have increased unemployment by over 4 per cent. It therefore follows that through those same economic policies we have increased stress related diseases by 20 per cent. In our health care system those diseases are expensive. That, I believe, is where a large part of the increases in health care costs in this country are coming from. They come directly out of the Minister of Finance's portfolio in the federal Government.
We should not be surprised at the increase in stress-related diseases, Mr. Speaker; it was predictable. I stood in this Chamber and predicted it on more than one occasion. I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the former Minister of Labour, now Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia), the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts), in one form or another, what they were going to do about the increased costs. The most common answer was that the prediction would not come true. There was no relationship between increased unemployment and increased incidence of stress-related diseases. It is 1984, Mr. Speaker, and it is now demonstrable that in fact these increases have been occurring. There is increased utilization of the health care system, which correlates well with the increased unemployment and increased economic hardship.
If the federal Government, and in particular the Minister of National Health and Welfare, want to take credit for doing something about the health care of Canadians, I do not think it will wash. We had the predictions going back to 1980, and we now have the record to look at. There has been no increased federal commitment to paying the bill for those increased health care costs. The federal Government, through its economic policies, has increased those costs but not its contribution. That leaves the Government in the best possible political position, because it does not have to take the political heat in meeting the increased need for services. It will push it off on the provinces.
April 2, 1984

The provinces have the responsibility to deliver the service and they have been scrambling the best they know how to handle those increased costs. Then the federal Government comes along and says that they have been doing it wrong. It does not tell them how to do it, it does not provide useful and positive suggestions for the future. It just tells them they have been doing it wrong. This issue, perhaps more than any other in the four years of this Parliament, should bring maximum concern to federal voters.
Any time you deal with health care, you deal with issues of life and death. Education and health care are two very large service delivery areas which the Canadian Constitution puts in the hands of the provinces. Unemployment increases the incidence of stress-related diseases and therefore increases costs in the health care system. But it also increases pressure on the educational system. Unemployed people choose to spend their time, if they can afford it, going to school instead of sitting around looking at the television set. Given that, the provinces have to face increased demand on the two largest budgetary items because of federal Government policies.
In that climate and over that period of time, what has the federal Government's response to those increased responsibilities and demands been? Cut back the funding! Make the formulas less generous. Make the transfer payments less adequate.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, in the closing stages of our debate on Bill C-3, it is time to put on record some information which may be useful to the new Members of Parliament who will be coming to the Chamber after the next election.
Liberals all.

Liberals all, says a backbencher on the other side. Hopefully, if it is Liberals, Mr. Speaker, it will be a different bunch with minds of their own, a willingness to learn about the issues and an ability to hold the Cabinet accountable. That would be a major change.
I would like to put on the record some of the things we must be concerned about in the future when we get a Cabinet which cares about something more than politics, which really cares about the health care of Canadians. Let us remember the concern with charges. Canadians are concerned that money may stand between them and their access to this system. That is what extra billing and user fees are about. A great many doctors tell us that the system is underfunded. That is variable from place to place, but there is evidence that there are not enough hospital beds. There are parts of the country where there are not enough well trained professional people. There are problems of underfunding. The nurses tell us there are some problems with the models we use and that we might be more effective and more efficient if we changed some of the models. Let us not forget that piece of advice and many others.
The provinces tell us we are going to go bankrupt unless we find better ways of controlling the costs. They may not be totally accurate, but there is a concern there to which politi-
Canada Health Act
cians of the future should pay attention and about which they could learn more. There is a common sense concern of patients as well as of medical professionals. They tell us that one of the reasons the system is having increased financial difficulty relates to administration. In so many fields of endeavour in Canada we put bigger and bigger proportions of expenditures into administration. Health care and education are two major examples. A smaller proportion of the dollars go into direct service and a larger portion goes into administration. Let us look at some of those issues.
If we really care about the issue of accessibility, let us tackle the problem of geography in this country. The quality of health care in a major Canadian city is of a different order than it is in some of our far-flung geographic regions. The quality of medical care which my children and family have enjoyed is a great deal different from the quality of health care on most Indian reservations even today. We have differences in accessibility which relate to geography, Mr. Speaker.
We have differences in accessibility which relate to consumer knowledge of how and when to purchase and when to go to a hospital. We can do a great deal more to educate our population in basic understanding of their own health so they know when and how best to access the health care system. We have a basic accessibility problem every time someone has to go on a waiting list. The more serious the concern and the longer the waiting list, the bigger the problem. That is a priority problem if we really care about accessibility.
I know my time is running out and the last problem I would like to speak about is the issue I raised a week ago, that is, the issue of the availability of well trained, committed professional people. If, in a legislative sense, we tell them that we do not value that choice, then the best, the brightest and the most committed will make another choice. That is the long-term danger in the inability of this Chamber and this Cabinet member to work with the provinces and with the profession to produce the kind of system we all need, want and should have.
