subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CONSEQUENCES OF WAR CRIMES PUBLICITY CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again, and for reasons best known to the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan), it is considered timely to launch a public campaign designed to draw attention to the fact that Canada may be harboring a number of Nazi war criminals and their collaborators.
Our legal statutes are not designed to deal with such crimes, particularly if they were committed in other countries, and, according to the Minister, no foreign country can be persuaded to request extradition in connection with a number of cases presently under investigation.
The Minister announced that deportation is being considered, a process which would have to be preceded by stripping the accused of their Canadian citizenship. This implies that we have two types of citizenship in this country, one that is inherited by birth, and another less valuable class which is obtained by choice.
As always, such public campaigns cast dark shadows of doubt and suspicion on the entire ethnic community in whose country of origin war crimes were committed. No one should ever permit memories of these hideous acts to be erased, but at the same time we cannot permit ourselves to be reminded of these events by acts of revenge directed against entire ethnic communities, many more members of which were victims of these crimes than were perpetrators.
I call on the Solicitor General of Canada and the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) to examine the role that Canada can play in dispensing justice with regard to these crimes, but I also call on them to dispense only such justice which is in our tradition. This would require that police inquiries be discreet, and that any persons against whom allegations are made be considered innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.
April 2, 1984

subtopic: NON PROFIT HOUSING ALLOCATIONS IN ONTARIO

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: NON PROFIT HOUSING ALLOCATIONS IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Liberal Government has demonstrated its strong commitment to meeting the needs of low and moderate income households through its funding of municipal and non profit housing programs. Unfortunately the Ontario Progressive Conservative Government does not share this commitment to assisting needy Canadians.
This year, with no warning, Ontario's Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing slashed the number of new non profit housing allocations from 250 in 1983 to 25 in 1984. This occurs at a time when the Ottawa Non-Profit Housing Corporation has a waiting list of 1,600 households requiring suitable and affordable housing.
The refusal of the Ontario Government to consult with the CMHC or municipalities over allocation of social housing units has played havoc with municipal budgets and has adversely affected the planning and staffing of Ottawa's NonProfit Housing Corporation.
In light of this irresponsible use of federal housing assistance, I join with Mayor Dewar of Ottawa and the Association of Municipalities of Ontario in calling for increased municipal consultation and control over the distribution of federal social housing units.
The municipalities of Ontario are better served by a Government committed to housing the low and moderate income earners not served by the private market in Ottawa. The present federal Government will maintain its commitment to providing affordable, suitable housing to these groups. To this end, I believe we should revert to a system whereby each municipal non profit housing corporation deals directly with the CMHC and a responsible and responsive federal Government.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CALL FOR ELIMINATION OF LOCKAGE FEES
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CALL FOR ELIMINATION OF LOCKAGE FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in April of 1959 the St. Lawrence Seaway opened with considerable fanfare and much expectation. Its opening marked the realization of a 400 year old dream. Over the years the canals were dug and the locks were built, overcoming the natural obstacles to navigation. Construction was spurred on by the desire to make this waterway the most economical route to move goods to and from the very heart of the North American continent.
The area affected by the St. Lawrence Seaway is larger than all of free Europe, and contains nearly one-third of the combined population of Canada and the United States. It is a tremendous market and a dream worthy of our earlier generation. Now, 25 years later, that foresight and spirit of enterprise are lacking.
In the earlier years traffic growth on the Seaway exceeded predictions. Seaway tolls kept increasing, and to force carriers to build larger ships, lockage fees were imposed.
In 1982 traffic declined to its lowest level since 1974. Twenty per cent of the cargo carriers did not even leave port in 1983. Traffic forecasts for this anniversary year are even less encouraging.
The economical advantage of this great waterway has slipped away. The key to long term improvement in the Seaway will be the elimination of the lockage fees and a substantial reduction in the tolls that are charged. Only then will we be able to look forward to a happy fiftieth anniversary.

subtopic: ONTARIO PROPOSAL TO ALTER UNIVERSITY CURRICULA

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ONTARIO PROPOSAL TO ALTER UNIVERSITY CURRICULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the role of the university in society has always been to provide the milieu and the environment for learning, exploring, and creating. Another function is to provide the manpower to meet the spiritual and material demands of an ever-changing and complex world. Modern universities must also adapt to accommodate an increasing enrolment and adjust their curricula to the needs of the time in order to provide a balanced educational experience.
Currently the Province of Ontario is contemplating, through a commission set up by the province's Minister of Education, to exercise greater control over its universities, to reform them administratively, and to alter the format of a wide based general education.
1 am very concerned that the Government of Ontario might be tempted to push most students, through alterations in university curricula, into specialized careers at the expense of a more generalized type of education. We do need specialists, there is no doubt about that, but we also need generalists with a broad based education, who can amalgamate the basic knowledge of many specialties.
Our society will be relying more and more on generalists with a background in critical thought to act as co-ordinators and leaders in our society. The Government of Ontario must recognize this, and not sacrifice the quality of the humanities and social science courses in our universities.

Mr. Speaker, today's appearance by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Mac-Guigan) before the panel of judges of the International Court of Justice in The Hague, where he will present Canada's case in the Gulf of Maine boundary dispute with the United States, focuses our attention on the dismal record of the Liberal Government in achieving internationally recognized and secure maritime boundaries for Canada. The Government has not only failed to establish agreed upon boundaries between Canada and the U.S.A. in the Gulf of Maine, but has also failed to resolve the Juan de Fuca Strait, Dixon Entrance, and Beaufort Sea disputes between the two countries.
Failure is not confined to negotiations with the U.S.A., but also is apparent in our relationships with Denmark over the Lincoln Sea, and with France over the St. Pierre-Miquelon area. Inconsistency of stance is apparent. For instance, the Government argues in favour of an equidistant line in the Gulf of Maine, but rejects it in the Beaufort Sea.
The effort to date has not been good enough. We must resolve these disputes so that Canada's borders will no longer be open to question, and fishermen and offshore resource developers can be sure of their rights and obligations.

difficult mission. As the first Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs to visit that part of the world, I wish him all success. May each step on the way be marked by clear and concrete initiatives in support of justice, development, and peace.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say something about Luigi Barzini who died over the weekend in Rome at the age of 75. Mr. Barzini was in many ways a modern renaissance figure. subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING SECOND WORLD WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister who will, no doubt, be aware that the Canadian public and the media are becoming increasingly favourable to an acknowledgment on the part of Parliament of the wrongdoings inflicted on Japanese Canadians in the course of the last War and after the War, notably expropriation and forced relocation. The Prime Minister will no doubt also be aware that the Special Committee on Visible Minorities just last week made unanimous recommendations with regard to an acknowledgment of the wrongdoings, a look at the War Measures Act, which was the Act that allowed those wrongdoings to occur, and the beginning of negotiations for compensation.
Will the Prime Minister undertake to introduce a resolution with regard to the acknowledgment of the wrongdoings, the re-examination of the War Measures Act, and the beginning of negotiations with representatives of the Japanese-Canadian community?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING SECOND WORLD WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot make that undertaking because I have not yet read the report of the committee which was tabled just last week. Knowing the people who worked on it, I know it is a serious report and I would certainly want to read it before making any decision. It would be a decision of Cabinet, and the matter has not been raised there.
If the Hon. Member is interested in my personal opinion, which is open to the possibility of change after reading the report and hearing the arguments, I am not inclined to envisage questions of compensation for acts which have perhaps discoloured our history in the past, if other means of redress are possible. I am not quite sure where we could stop the compensating. I know that we would have to go back a great length of time in history and look at all of the injustices which have occurred, perhaps beginning with the deportation of the Acadians and going on to the treatment of the Chinese Canadians in the late 19th century. I do not believe in attempting to rewrite history in this way.
On other occasions I have personally expressed to Japanese Canadians the regret that I feel about the terrible acts which happened to them. There is no justification for them after the
fact.
To me this is in the category of those who want to rehabilitate Riel. Riel stands as he stands. I do not see that there is
Oral Questions
much to gain by trying to apologize for acts of our greatgrandfathers and their great-grandfathers.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I wonder if we could at least have a commitment to an early date to get a resolution, if Cabinet does agree to it. We are concerned when we hear that there cannot be any discussion of a particular injustice until all injustices are dealt with. This certainly would take time that we would not want to contemplate. People are concerned that this not go on and on. If the Prime Minister has not discussed it in Cabinet, certainly the recommendation has been made over the years. My Party has raised this issue.
I wonder if we could at least have a commitment that we will get a resolution on the matters with which we can proceed. It is true that compensation is a matter that would have to be discussed, as to amount and kind, collective or individual. The community itself is not agreed on that. We could go ahead, however, with an acknowledgment on the part of Parliament, which we have not yet had, and we could go ahead on an agreement to re-examine the War Measures Act-that is within our power-to see that the Act is within the spirit of the Charter of Rights.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, insofar as the War Measures Act is concerned, the Charter of Rights does supersede it in its own language. I am certain that the kind of actions that we regret would not be justified or condoned by the courts in the future. Therefore, we have brought in redress, for our time and for the future, to the most unacceptable type of acts which have happened in the past.
Returning to the question of compensation, as the Hon. Member knows, we are going back to the earliest part of our historic times in Canada and we are beginning to look at the question of treaties with the aboriginal peoples. We are negotiating settlement of those treaties. I do not know if the next step will be to jump over a few centuries to the Japanese Canadians, or if we should not stop at the deportation of the Acadians on the way, and realize that there is not too much to gain in Canada by trying once again to correct the economic consequences of unjust acts committed in the past to whole groups, rather than trying to be just in our time. I find it more important to be just in our time, for instance, by giving jobs with the money to the people who are unemployed now, rather than trying to use that money to compensate people whose ancestors in some way have been deprived.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-3, an Act relating to cash contributions by Canada in respect of insured health services provided under provincial health care insurance plans and amounts payable by Canada in respect of extended health care services and to
April 2, 1984
amend and repeal certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, the Canada Health Act will accomplish a number of things. As the traditional supporters of medicare, indeed as the originators through our predecessors, the CCF, we are very glad to see the improvements brought about in this Bill. It will address the crisis in medicare of extra billing and user fees.
It is true that medicare has been under threat, partly because of federal expenditure cutbacks on medicare, partly on account of provincial cutbacks, and partly on account of ideological reluctance to deal with medicare issues on the part of some of the provinces. We have seen the threat of moving to a two-tier system with specialized, quality care and a range of services available to those who can pay for them and for basic services for those who are not able to pay user fees and extra billing. In other words, we are moving to a system entirely contrary to what was originally envisaged, that of quality care for all in a truly universal system.
This two-tier system, which we are trying to correct with the legislation before us, is an inefficient and expensive system. What will happen is that people who are unable to pay the extra bills will have to go to a system of private insurance to do so. Unions will negotiate private insurance schemes to cover the services for which a person has to pay extra. Then we would have a system in the public sector covering the basic services and one in the private sector, with its additional layer of administrative costs as well as the costs reflected in profits, because this would be run by the private sector on the basis of whatever money they could get out of the system.
The United States has this kind of two-tier system with a very large profit-oriented private sector, and we know the results are that health care services are expensive. They pay a higher proportion of their GNP for medical costs than we do and fewer people are covered. Therefore, the system we have developed in Canada is one that we can really be proud of. It is an excellent system which stands up very well in international comparisons and which is a relatively efficient and cost-effective system. Naturally we think it can be improved and we have introduced amendments, some of which have been accepted and some of which have not. We want to have it even more cost-effective and responsive to people's needs. But, by and large, it is a good, efficient and effective system. We have a good system, we want to face the crisis, confront the two-tier system, address the crisis and solve it.
This is a better Bill, Mr. Speaker, as a result of a number of amendments introduced by the NDP caucus. We fought for them, and some of them were accepted. We did not get all we wanted but we brought a couple of extremely important provisions into the legislation at committee stage. We want to see our medicare system become a truly health care system. It should not just provide treatment after the fact, but also should include preventive services, including the services of paraprofessionals for the quality care they can offer.
Canada Health Act
In light of that we asked for a number of amendments, and let me quote one. The door has been opened with the following improvement in the wording:
The health care insurance plan of a province must insure all insured health services provided by hospitals, medical practitioners or dentists, and-
This is the addition:
-where the law of the province so permits, similar or additional services rendered by other health care practitioners.
In other words, the provinces may bring into their system additional health care professionals and they may have expenses covered by our new Canada Health Act when it is passed. It will encourage a province to make use of other health care professionals. This means that we will be getting better care and a better range of options for people to enable them to make decisions about the kind of care they want. Health care professionals other than doctors usually provide their services at a somewhat lower fee, so we will end up with the best of both worlds. We will have more cost-efficient medical care and care which people want. They will be able to choose what they want and will get savings in costs in the overall system.
We hope that paramedical services, nurse practitioners and other professionals will come in as well. The nurses have lobbied very extensively for this and the New Democratic Party has supported their endeavours and will continue to support endeavours to include these health care professionals in our system. We had hoped to get general inclusion of these practitioners, but at least we have the door open so that we will be ready to accept them when the provinces allow them to come in.
We have a broader concept of health accepted in the legislation by an amendment to the preamble, which reads as follows:
-that Canadians can achieve further improvements in their well-being through combining individual lifestyles that emphasize fitness, prevention and health promotion with collective action against the social, environmental and occupational causes of disease, and that they desire a system of health services that will promote such physical, and mental health and such protection against disease;
That is a good philosophical statement which tries to show where we want to go and that health care is not only the avoidance of disease but also the promotion of health through prevention good nutrition, better lifestyles, exercise and cleaning up of occupational health hazards. All of these things are part of it. This is something to which a whole community can contribute by taking collective action to improve the environment, the air we breathe and the working environment.
The New Democratic Party continued to press for other amendments, which I am sorry to say were not accepted. I would like to mention a few of these to show the direction in which we would like the Canada Health Act to go. One of the most important of these is a provision for the escalation of penalties. One of the most important functions of this Act is to provide for penalties so that the federal Government can respond to extra billing and user fees of a province, not just by cutting them off completely, which would not be acceptable to

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
the Canadian public and which would make too many people suffer as a result, but to give greater flexibility. The New Democratic Party is concerned that the dollar for dollar withholding of subsidies for health care would not be adequate to discourage extra billing and user fees on the part of a province. We proposed that the withholding of dollar for dollar hold only for the first year of the penalty, that it go up to $2 for every dollar allowed in extra billing and user fees in the second year, and in the third year that it escalate to $3 for every dollar misused in health care expenditures. Our feeling is that these more adequate penalties would give the federal Government more clout in dealing with the provinces and would still give it adequate flexibility.
An important amendment, which was unfortunately ruled out of order, is that moneys which are withheld as penalties, apart from those that would be returned if the province cleaned up its act, got rid of extra billing and got the money back, should be redirected to provinces which are complying with the Act. These moneys would be used to facilitate research, innovation and service development in areas of alternative health care, delivery systems and preventive and medical health promotions. The idea is that if provinces are not living up to the spirit and letter of the Canada Health Act they should be penalized and lose this money. We do not want this money to go just anywhere. This money is supposed to be devoted to health care. Let us put it where it would do some good. Let us give it to the provinces that are complying with the Act and that would put that money into special innovative programs that would be of benefit to all Canadians. Let us allow the provinces that are living up to the spirit and terms of the Canada Health Act to get some benefit from that. That benefit would not be confined to their own citizens but would have effects throughout the country. People in other provinces would see the good things that happen as a result of these innovative programs.
Another amendment on which the Conservatives voted with us, but which was unfortunately defeated by the Government, was that no penalty would come into force until passed by Parliament. This would provide for public debate before any penalties were actually meted out. Therefore, it would not be a matter of Cabinet discretion only, a matter which would be dealt with privately and secretly, but it would be a matter for open, public debate. When the Canada Health Act is being violated by a province we certainly need public debate. That would perhaps be an effective way of dealing with it. It would certainly help to get the issue before the public so that people in the provinces concerned would know very clearly what was happening.
We lost an amendment to ensure an acceptable ratio of ward to private and semi-private accommodation in hospitals. We are very concerned that there be quality care in our hospitals and that this quality care be available not only to those who can pay extra to get semi-private or private care. Good quality care ought to be available to all Canadians, even if they cannot afford the extra costs to get private or semi-private care. Unfortunately that amendment was not passed.
We are at a very important juncture in our health care system. I would like, therefore, to spend a few minutes looking back as well as forward to see the unfolding and how the different ideas were brought into medicare in Canada to give us some idea of what are the next steps we should be taking. I am proud to do this because it was my colleagues in the old CCF, and later in the NDP, who pioneered most of the elements of the medicare system. In 1945, with a very new CCF Government, Saskatchewan was the first to introduce medical and dental care for all old age pensioners and for mothers' allowance recipients and their families. That was a very small beginning for the people most in need, but is was a noticeable beginning for our system. In 1945, a federal-provincial discussion on tax arrangements to facilitate an extension of this program was unsuccessful. It was not until very much later that there was another important and comprehensive amendment to medicare.
In 1948, the Saskatchewan CCF Government introduced an experimental government-sponsored medical care plan in one region of the province. This included a full range of medical services and dental care for children under 16. The following year, again under the CCF Government, Saskatchewan became the first province to introduce comprehensive government-sponsored hospital insurance. This is one of the most costly items in our health care system. In 1957, the federal Government passed the Hospital and Diagnostic Services Act, which provides for federal cost sharing of hospital services. It was only a few years later that all provinces took advantage of this.
In one province we can see the pioneer work being done beginning in the 1940s. It took quite a long time before other provinces and the federal Government became convinced to act. In 1961, Mr. Justice Emmett Hall was appointed to chair the Royal Commission on Health Services. This, of course, was the commission that recommended our full medicare system. In 1962, Saskatchewan became the first province to introduce a comprehensive provincially sponsored medical prepayment plan and fought it out with a doctors' strike. If it had not been for the courage of the CCF Government in Saskatchewan we would not have medicare today. In 1964, the Hall Commission reported, recommending a comprehensive medical insurance plan. In 1966, with a minority Government, the Medical Care Act was passed providing for 50 per cent federal cost sharing. By 1971, the last province, New Brunswick, joined the medical care plan. We can see the beginning of medicare in 1945 in a CCF province, and finally in a Conservative province in 1971. While the last province with a Conservative regime joined medicare in 1971, in 1973 the NDP provincial government were introducing more innovations. In 1973, Manitoba introduced Canada's first universal pharmacare program for seniors and universal nursing home care. In 1974, Manitoba with an NDP government became the first province to introduce a government dental care plan for children. Also in 1974, Saskatchewan with an NDP government became the first province to offer no cost aids to the handicapped.
April 2, 1984

Again we can see that Conservative provinces have come along rather more reluctantly while CCF and NDP provinces were very much in the forefront in bringing in innovations.
There is much discussions now of a national consensus on medicare. I am certainly pleased to see that all three Parties support the current Canada Health Act, but it is very clear in this national consensus that some are active members and leaders in fighting for medicare while others are rather slow converts to the cause and are rather reluctant in seeing the benefits of having a comprehensive medical care system. While the Conservatives are not in the forefront of supporting medicare, they are not fighting it. Unfortunately, there is some backlash against medicare on the part of the National Citizens' Coalition.
I suppose all Members of the House have been receiving, as well as seeing in the newspapers, a lot of nonsense on the issue of medicare. They are very misleading statements on the part of this so called National Citizens' Coalition. I want to mention a few of them and point out what is so ludicrously wrong with the kind of propaganda they are putting out. For instance, they ask, "Do you really want someone who has been forced into adopting a civil servant mentality doing open heart surgery on you or delivering your baby?" They state:
Waiting lines for surgery are going to get much longer and because literally thousands of highly educated and talented specialists will be reluctantly driven out of our country there will be fewer doctors. Those who are left will be eventually reduced to clock watching.
More Canadians will die because they can't get the life-saving health care they need, when they need it.
When they say that doctors will be turned into a bunch of civil servants, I would like to point out to anyone who is interested in this kind of claptrap that this is simply untrue. How a person is paid does not determine whether that person is qualified, experienced, able, dedicated or conscientious. People can be all of these things and indeed even be civil servants. It is quite possible.
I have lived in other countries where there are actually civil servants who are doctors and where health care is indeed of extremely high quality. It depends on their training, experience and dedication, which is quite independent from how they are paid.
I am sorry to hear statements like this being made because it is a scare tactic which might give people the wrong impression. I know that this body is not dealing with the real problems before us concerning the health care system, which is extending it to include paraprofessionals, the issue of midwifery and home births, and the issue of community health care clinics. These are all ways of improving our health care system.
This group also seems to be very reluctant to note that having a profit motive in medicine can be a danger as well. They say that people would not want a civil servant operating on them, but I would not want somebody operating on me who is in it strictly for profits and will recommend the most expensive intervention because it is the most profitable. There-
Canada Health Act
fore, there are dangers as well in having too much of a profit motive in the medicare system. We have seen evidence of this in other countries. There are many useless operations being done in the United States where there is too much of a profit motive.
To conclude let me just say that we have gone a long way to get to this Canada Health Act. I am pleased to see it and will certainly vote for it. I want to assure the House that the NDP caucus will continue to work and be in the forefront of reform in Canada's health services to see that Canadians get the kind of health care they want.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a ten minute period for questions or comments. If there are no questions or comments, the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) on debate.

Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to review Bill C-3, which enacts the new Canada Health Act, in the context of all the history that has preceded the introduction of this legislation in the House of Commons. Let me begin by characterizing the new Canada Health Act in this way; if a government has many crises relating to unemployment, such as rising interest rates and all those matters which affect Canadians in their day-to-day lives, and it cannot solve any of those crises, then it may be advisable to create a crisis that affects each and every Canadian that it can then pretend or purport to solve.
Essentially, that is what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Government have done in bringing in Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act. The Government has said that there is a problem with health care across Canada, that we are losing universality of our health care system. But the Government tells Canadians not to worry because it will save them from this threat.
I have talked to members of the medical profession, including surgeons, nurses and everyone involved in the health care system. They never saw the problem in that way. No one ever asked me to go back to Ottawa to try to preserve the universality of our health care system. What I was told time and again was to go back to Ottawa and make sure that the Government of Canada fulfills its commitment to Canada's health care system by providing adequate funds to preserve and advance the health care system that we now have in place.
There is not a professional in the health care system who does not see the problem of medical care as involving funding. In other words, the problems that exist in the health care system are the result of underfunding. It is as simple as that.
But what happened? The Government wants to forget about the facts and deal with the perception. It wants to deal with the idea, which it has built up over a period of time, that there is a problem. This has been done particularly by the Minister of National Health and Welfare with the little pamphlets she has sent out in the mail to innocent Canadians. These pamphlets, which they read while opening their cheques or waiting in long line-ups at the banks, tell them that there is a problem. If people are told about it long enough and read about it long

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
enough they will eventually believe that there is a problem and believe that a piece of legislation is necessary to solve that problem.
That is what we are doing here. We are dealing with a myth, a ghost. We are trying to deal with a piece of legislation that purports to solve a problem that does not exist. While the Government is not very smart, it is not totally stupid and has introduced a couple of concepts to help create this myth which it has developed over a period of years. It used two words that have become anathema to many Canadians. The two terms which it has developed are extra billing and user fees. Those great evils of the health system, extra billing and user fees, are used as though extra billing and user fees were totally unconnected to the problem of underfunding of the health care system.
I do not believe that anyone on either side of the House of Commons or in any of the provincial chambers across the country wants to have user fees or extra billing for patients who are the consumers of the health care services. We all want a totally free system, but the problem is how to pay for it. Where will the money come from to pay for the system? Those provinces that do not have the wealth and resources that are required to pay for the system must, in some cases, resort to user fees or some other method of collecting medical fees. The common method is extra billing.
To make the claim that extra billing and user fees are evils in themselves, unconnected with the government funding of Canada's medical health services, is a pretence. It is a worse than a pretence, it is a fraud because there is an illicit motive behind it. The Minister of National Health and Welfare who presides over this massive health system knows better. She must know that the only reason for having user fees and extra billing in any of the provinces in Canada is to raise money to help provide the health care services that are part of the system. Yet she isolates them and says that they are evil and an attack upon universality. Nothing could be further from the truth.
In this House of Commons we are constantly fighting the Government's attempt to create perceptions instead of presenting the facts. This is one more case, and we have to fight it. However, the trouble and the difficulty is that we, like everyone else in Canada, want the health care system preserved in its entirety and improved. We all want that. What is this pretense of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) that there are people out to attack Canada's health care system and that we on this side of the House want sick Canadians, not well Canadians? That is as ridiculous in reality as it is in the speaking. There is not a grain of truth in that, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare knows it, as does every Member of the House.
The problem is with the quality of health care in Canada. It is as simple as that. What kind of a health care system do we want? What kind of medical personnel do we want in our hospitals? What kind of equipment do we want in operating
rooms when we go in for surgery? What kind of hospital beds do we want? Do we want automatic hospital beds or ones that crank up? All these things are part of the system. They have to be decided in each and every instance. But what has to be taken as the general guide is: Do we want a health care system which is the equal of any of the advanced nations in the western world or, for that matter, in the eastern world or in the whole world? If we ask that question of thinking Canadians, they will respond immediately by saying, "We want the best possible health care system. Give us the best possible health care system in the circumstances and then we as Canadians will find ways to pay for it".
I happen to have a long exposure to the matter of health care in Canada. I was a junior solicitor in the Department of the Attorney General in Nova Scotia in the late fifties when hospital care was introduced. I can tell the House that that was a traumatic experience for the then Stanfield Government of Nova Scotia, because Mr. Stanfield and his colleagues in his Cabinet knew that hospital care would be an enormous expense for the Province of Nova Scotia. In 1984-85 that is proven by the fact that the Province of Nova Scotia spends 24.5 per cent of its total budget on health. One quarter in every dollar spent by the Government of Nova Scotia is in health services. Mr. Stanfield knew in the late fifties what a burden hospital care would be on the people and taxpayers of Nova Scotia. He thought long and hard about it, but Nova Scotia opted in because it was recognized that there was nothing more important than the health of its citizens. There is nothing more important to Nova Scotia than that the province have healthy citizens. That can be said of every part of Canada. There is nothing more important than the personal health of individuals.
As you get to my age, Mr. Speaker, you realize more and more every day that you value among everything you might possess your own personal health. Once again let me underline the fact that nobody is here to hurt in any way, shape or form our health care system. The problem is: How do we finance it and at what level do we operate, that is to say, at what level of patient care?
Notwithstanding the statistics presented, there has been in fact a decrease in funding emanating from the Government of Canada to the provinces. That is simply stated in the table provided by the Province of Nova Scotia which shows very clearly that the transfer payments from the Government of Canada in 1984-85 were 40.6 per cent of the revenues, that is the total recoveries of the Province of Nova Scotia. In 1983-84 that figure was 43.5 per cent. It is going down. They can come up with whatever numbers they want in the House of Commons and elsewhere, but the fact of the matter is that federal contributions to the provinces, particularly the Province of Nova Scotia, are going down.
Let us not fool around and juggle statistics around trying to fool people. It comes out at the other end. There is a bottom line. The bottom line is in the hospitals, the doctors' offices and everywhere else where we have to pay for health care. The dollar bills are not there. We can see it in the cracked walls, in
April 2, 1984

the rusty equipment and everywhere we go. I have to say to members of the Liberal Party who insist in the House that the Canada Health Act is an improvement that they should travel to the hospitals and to the outlets of health care, and they will see that there is no improvement. The evidence is very clear and cogent that the health care service in Canada is degenerating. It is going down. There is not a professional medical person practising in Nova Scotia who would argue against that.
Someone said that this is really a matter of political power, that this has nothing to do with health or health care services, that it is simply the Government of Canada exercising its pre-eminence in the health care field, as it has pushed people and provinces out of the energy field, the resource field and every other field which it seeks to occupy. Under the British North America Act there is a theory of occupied field. The Parliament of Canada can come in and occupy a particular field in the interests of all Canadians. But our Government is not doing it that way, directly, and saying, "We want the health care field totally under the control of the federal Government". It is just doing it in this almost nefarious way, saying, "We have the dollar bills. We have the strength. We are the ones who do not have to provide health care". The federal Government does not have to treat a patient. It does not have to provide a hospital bed, but if it is to do it, it wants total control. The only way to do that is through legislation of the purse-strings, and that is why we have this Bill before us. If the provinces give up in this fight-and they are apparently giving up for reasons I will mention-then the federal Government is in complete control.
Let me tell the House about one of the saddest features of the Canada Health Act. I have some 25 years of personal experience in this behind me. Do you know who that is? It is the so-called hero of Canadian medical care, Dr. Emmett Hall, in his older age. I have the greatest respect for our senior citizens, but the fact of the matter is that Judge Hall is a retired judge of the Supreme Court, retired because of reaching the mandatory age limit. Does that mean his judgment is suspect? No, not in all cases, because some of our citizens of that age have keener minds than many of us. But in the case of Judge Hall you have to suspect something, and I want to put that right on the floor of the House of Commons. Judge Hall has said-
We are starting to suspect you.
-that time goes by for all of us, as younger Members will find out. He says that the medical profession in Canada cannot become a law unto itself. Judge Hall said, and listen to this-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Why did you mention his age? What does that have to do with it?

-that the medical profession has been granted a monopoly to practise medicine to the exclusion of all others. Thank God the Minister of National Health and Welfare cannot practise medicine. Thank God somebody has said that
Canada Health Act
medical practitioners are the only ones permitted to practise medicine. What kind of nonsense is that from the father of medical care, that the medical profession has been granted a monopoly?
It reminds me of a cartoon which I saw-and I address this particularly to the Minister of National Health and Welfare- of a sick lady lying in bed and an obvious witch-doctor standing at the end of the bed, and the husband saying, "It is the only person who would take housecalls". That is what is happening here when you pretend that the medical profession has some kind of monopoly. Oh, they are going to take us, just because I cannot practise medicine, just because the Minister of National Health and Welfare cannot practise medicine! This group which has been granted an exclusive privilege will take advantage of us! What nonsense. What an utter sham. It is totally ridiculous. I cannot believe that it is happening.
The medical profession has not been granted any monopoly. The medical profession is made up of the people who by training over a long period of time have proved their capability and capacity to perform certain acts connected with what we call the practise of medicine. There is no mystery to it. If one wants to be a doctor, one goes to medical school. One qualifies, obtains a diploma and certification and becomes a doctor.
Judge Hall is a doctor too, but not that kind of doctor, thank God. I want to say that I think this is one of the worst things in this whole debate. Somebody at the level of Mr. Justice Hall, the father of medical care, so-called in Canada, said that the medical profession has a monopoly to practice and they are using it against the people of Canada. Enough of that nonsense. Some of my best friends and close associates are medical doctors.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Nobody would have thought of that.

There is a remark from the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I am supposed to feel embarrassed because I know some people in the medical profession. Why would I feel embarrassed? That is one of the proudest claims I can make. I have a great many friends in the medical profession. I see them socially and otherwise. I am proud of them. I do not think there is any higher calling in our society. How do you like that, Mrs. Minister or whatever you are called.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is Madam.

One of those medical doctors, who happens to be a provincial public servant of many years' standing, the head of one of our best medical institutions in Nova Scotia, has written this speech for me. It is a personal message from him to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He said in his letter:
I want you to express these views in the House of Commons.
His views are so well expressed that I will simply quote what he said. He said:
As proposed, I am concerned that Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act, will threaten the availability and quality of medical care in Canada, that it will

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
cripple a health care system that has been recognized as one of the best in the world and will interfere with the economic professional freedom of the medical profession.
This is from a medical doctor in Nova Scotia who has been an employee of the Province of Nova Scotia for years. He goes on to say:
The Canada Health Act is supposed to amalgamate, update and more clearly redefine the conditions of current federal legislation and the Medical Care Act of 1966. These have been legislative instruments by which Ottawa has provided funding for provincial health care programs, but if the Minister of National Health and Welfare's proposal is accepted, it will do more than that.
Here are the specific points that he lists. He said the Bill will:
Convert Canada's high quality health care insurance program into state medicine,
Make the serious under-funding of the situation even worse,
Reduce the ability of hospitals to meet the needs of communities they serve, Reduce the financial flexibility of provincial governments and their ability to finance health care,
Widen the disparities and the availability and quality of health care service that exists between provinces and communities,
Deny patients the democratic right to buy health care services that they need or want beyond those provided by the state,
Interfere with patients' rights to obtain health services from physicians and hospitals of their choice-
Deny physicians the right to deal directly with their patients to establish the value of our service and thus reduce our economic freedom.
In short, what he says and what I agree with is that the Act is a sham. It is a device to get federal control. It is a device to contend that the Government of Canada, under the Minister of National Health and Welfare, is solving the health care problems of Canada.
Everybody is put in a difficult position. We support the health care system in Canada. We support medicare. We support hospital care for all Canadians. Only a few months ago I had occasion to require care in hospital. I told the Minister of National Health and Welfare about that. I wanted, as all Canadians do when they enter hospital, the best care possible; otherwise you will pay for it afterwards. That is what Canadians want. They want the highest quality of health care. Our duty is to provide the opportunity for all Canadians to get the best possible health care that the system can deliver. That is our purpose. We cannot do that if we simply obstruct the Canada Health Act before this Parliament. We cannot do that by just blocking it. We can expose the errors of the ways of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. We can expose her attitude and the contempt that she shows for the deliverers of health care services. However, to vote against the Bill that provides health care for Canadians is another matter.
I want to end on one note in the case of Nova Scotia just to show everybody in this Parliament and elsewhere what kind of a person we are dealing with in the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Nova Scotia medical practitioners receive 85 per cent of the approved fee. They have received that fee since medical health care was introduced. It is part of an agreement they made with the province and with the Government of Canada. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is simply revoking that and saying that that historic fact
goes out the window, "you get whatever you get and that's it". She calls that extra billing. She is wrong about that and she is wrong about most everything else she says about medical care in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I make no apologies. You put me on a rack and I will not give you the name of the doctor who wrote to me. If there is a rule in this House of Commons that can require you to deliver confidential material, I tell you that I am not going to obey that rule. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Hon. Member tell us why in referring to Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, before his derogatory comments concerning Mr. Justice Hall, he prefaced them by saying he was retired and somewhat up in years? I do not quote him exactly, but I think the reference is clear.

Mr. Speaker, I think the references are clear. I do not believe that anybody has given medical practitioners a monopoly. That is not the nature of the law at all. If Mr. Justice Hall thinks they have been given a monopoly, all I can say is that he is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member made an unwarranted attack on Mr. Justice Emmett Hall. I submit he took out of context what Mr. Justice Hall had to say about a monopoly. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall was talking about expanding our present medical and hospital services. He talked about paramedics, home nursing, midwives, nurses, a whole host of things in the area of preventive medicine. Up until now, the medical profession has had a monopoly on most of that. The Hon. Member could not carry water for Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, who is the father of medicare and hospitalization in Canada. He brought in the royal commission report; it was him, Tommy Douglas and Woodrow Lloyd. By the way, it was not the Hon. Member's Party, although Mr. Justice Hall was a supporter of that Party. He was never a supporter of our Party. It was Mr. Justice Hall who helped father this program in Canada and who calls for the expansion of it. The medical profession does have a monopoly. They have too damned much say. They have a monopoly licensing authority and a monopoly
April 2, 1984

union. The Hon. Member owes an apology to Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, and he had better make it now.

If I owe anyone an apology, I will apologize. However, I will start with the allegation that I quoted out of context. I quoted from a newspaper which was delivered just one week ago. I will now quote from a newspaper report dated December 10, 1983, in which Mr. Justice Emmett Hall was reported as having spoken before the Health Coalition of Nova Scotia, a group financed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to lobby for her Canada Health Act. That report quoted Mr. Justice Hall as saying:
A physician is not only a medical person ... he said.
"He has moral and social obligations as well as self-interest... the medical profession is a monopoly created by the state ... the state will prosecute anyone who is not licensed to act in that field"-
Let me ask the Hon. Member what that means.

speechtext: Just to be clear, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) but questions are supposed to be directed to the person who made the speech.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member if it was not correct that the former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), appointed Mr. Justice Emmett Hall to do a review of our medicare and hospitalization system, as a result of which Mr. Justice Emmett Hall made a certain number of recommendations to do away with what he calls the monopoly of the medical profession over the other services that can be provided which are presently governed by, ordered by, prescribed by or requested by a member of the medical profession. How do you know what he was talking about?

I ask the Hon. Member if it is not correct that Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, in the context of his remarks about the monopoly, was perfectly correct and that he is calling for an expansion of the kinds of people who provide medical and health services. Is that not what Mr. Justice Emmett Hall recommended to the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead?

Mr. Speaker, I think I could make my position very clear without the distortions of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) or any other Member in the House. Mr. Justice Hall, as I said very clearly in my speech, is the so-called father of medical care. I walked around Nova Scotia with Mr. Justice Emmett Hall when he went there to study medical care and to write the report that he eventually published. No one has to tell me about Mr. Justice Hall.
I am trying to point out that over a period of time, Mr. Justice Hall changed his view. He suddenly got the idea that the enemy of medical care was the medical profession. This is a very hurtful view. He said that the medical profession has a
Canada Health Act
monopoly. The medical profession does not have a monopoly. That is not what a monopoly is. He has repeated it time and time again and fostered the whole idea that the medical profession is doing this or is doing that. In the newspaper article to which I referred before, Mr. Justice Hall is quoted as saying:
"When the state gives a monopoly of that kind ... gives the right to deliver an essential service, the state becomes automatically involved."
That is simply not true, Mr. Speaker. I cannot help it if Mr. Justice Emmett Hall said it, or a prince or a pauper said it; it is simply not true. I am trying to say that that kind of mistaken attitude leads to a great many other false conclusions, the most important of which is that the medical profession does not have certain rights. Those rights, if taken away, must be taken away in a fair manner. A provision of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is that if one takes something away, one must give something in return.
In the case of the medical health profession in Nova Scotia, the Canada Health Act has taken away the medical practitioner's privilege that existed under the law of Nova Scotia to bill for the difference between the 85 per cent of the approved fee and the approved fee. That privilege may be wiped out because of the Canada Health Act. It may be wiped out by a recommendation of Mr. Justice Hall who said that these doctors had a monopoly and that the state was involved so the state could take it away.
I do not accept that kind of philosophy. I do not accept it and I am sorry to run into conflict with the father of medical care, but I stated my position very clearly. I will argue it before any group. I do not agree that the medical profession has the kind of monopoly suggested by Mr. Justice Hall, and I think that that is the cause of a huge problem in Canada, a problem that will plague us for decades to come.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is the conclusion of the 10-minute period for questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, as I was listening to the interchange between the last two speakers, I was reminded of the fact that, indeed, the medical profession cannot be a monopoly because there are so many fast operators in other areas of Canadian life. I think the point of view expressed by some Hon. Members of the NDP and, indeed, of the Government Party is testimony to the fact that one can operate in several ways. One can operate from a level of political concern and a sense of justice, or one can operate from a position of trying to gain political advantage.
I have several major points I would like to make. Before beginning, I would like to confirm, as have all members of the Conservative Opposition, the fact that I will be voting for this Bill because there are many principles embodied in this Bill which we feel are important. As described by the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), medical care is a sacred trust which first began in the days of John Diefenbaker and Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, something that we as a Party very firmly believe is important to the mainstream of Canadian life,

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
and something which is the responsibility of all governments to provide to Canadian citizens.
I am certainly not a disinterested party in this debate. Indeed, I can remember in my first days of medical practice the great relief that existed when it was made clear that a patient who required hospitalization had hospital insurance, and the frustration and difficulties that were encountered when a patient was not able to be brought into hospital for what in many cases was necessary treatment because he could not afford to pay a hospital bill. These are things for which we have a responsibility as a Government across Canada.
There are two main issues that arise. We have established the principles of universality, reasonable accessibility, comprehensiveness, portability of benefits and non-profit administration. These principles have been established, but they have been added to by the Act we are seeing now, and this identifies one of my major areas of concern.
This morning when questioning the Hon. Member for Pro-vencher who entered into debate on this Bill, the Minister indicated that the provincial Governments had created additional health care costs for themselves because they were providing medical care facilities to small communities they administer throughout the provinces. I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that this identifies very clearly something all of us should pay attention to, and something all of us should take note of for the future. If this indicates that the Minister of Health feels that that is not an appropriate expenditure, then she indeed is the one who is threatening the type of health care that we in Canada have come to expect and would like to see in the future.
We are not dealing with downtown Toronto, downtown Montreal or downtown Quebec City. We are dealing with the small rural areas of Canada where Canadian people are employed in areas of low population density, or in the farthest reaches of our territories. It is those people for whom we must provide care of the highest level possible. The Minister indicates that she would be critical of a provincial Government that was attempting to provide that level of care, and she has clearly indicated that where it is her repsonsibility she has not provided that care.
The visibility factor as it is dealt with in the Bill indicates in general the Minister's approach to the health care scene. She has included in the Act a requirement that the federal Government be more visible. For the most part, if we are able to do good deeds it would be nice to be recognized for them. But if we require recognition in anticipation of good deeds, and if that becomes a premise for bringing forward legislation, then that is a sad testimony to the type of government we have in Canada.
The Minister has spent $3 million to advertise the Canada Health Act. We understand that it takes between $25,000 and $50,000 to support one life, and beyond that it strains the level of care that we are able to provide. Indeed, we lose lives because we cannot provide the necessary support systems. Mr. Speaker, $3 million would potentially have maintained 60 Canadian lives. Yet that is what the Minister has spent on advertising this program, separate from anything to do with the actual delivery, administration and provision of health care to Canadians. That is the style of government we have in Canada. It is a style of government which is geared to maintaining power; it is a style of government that is non-productive and does not get to the heart of many issues that need to be dealt with.
The second major point I should like to make is one that I probably feel more strongly about than do many other Members. That is not to say that I feel I can explain or understand it completely, or that I will be an expert on it; it is only to say that I speak from probably a perspective that is important to consider at this stage of the debate. This concerns the future of the medical care system in Canada.
A mentality is developing that concerns me greatly, Mr. Speaker. If the Minister has any interest in the health care system in Canada she will be interested in it as well. A mentality is developing in the medical profession based on the insecurity, the concerns and the grievances it has with the Minister and with governments at all levels when they do not maintain contracts, when they impose settlements, when they arrive at conclusions separate and apart from the considerations that have been brought forward, when they put the profession in the position where it feels it no longer has the rights and freedoms it needs-the professional freedom, the freedom as Canadians to live and practise medicine in Canada in a way that they believe to be in the best interests of their patients and their country.
I do not offer this lightly, Mr. Speaker. Hon. Members opposite may smile and I know I can be accused of self-interest, but it is a mentality that is growing. It is a type of mentality that prompts my colleagues to say to me "Why don't you provide us with full state medicine? Why should I get up at five o'clock in the afternoon-we all know that government offices usually close between four and four-thirty in the afternoon, so why should I go on a call at five o'clock, or six or seven or eight o'clock at night if I am going to be managed by a bureaucracy, with all the obligations and none of the benefits?" That is the mentality that is spreading in the profession. It will be expensive for Canadians in future in terms of the type of medical care they can expect and will receive. I have not got an answer for that because I cannot answer for the Minister's intentions in the Bill or how she intends to operate the system across Canada from a central bureaucracy, when the Government cannot even meet the requirements of individual communities. I do not know how the Minister is going to manage that, but I can understand the concern of the professionals.
This is not really a concern for politicians, Mr. Speaker, and certainly not for the Minister who will always get the level of health care that she wants. It is not a concern for me either because I can look after myself. It is a concern for Canadian citizens. Their destiny may well be integrated into a system that is being run by people who do not have personal involve-
April 2, 1984

ment and whose dedication has been struck away because of abuse and the level of control that may be exercised by this or some other Minister. We all hope that will not happen. But I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a growing mentality in the medical profession in Canada today. It is the sum and substance of the letters I have received, and the personal conversations I have had.
Those are the two major points I would like to contribute to the debate, Mr. Speaker. Other Members have spoken of the broad general concerns and major issues of financing, and attitudes which they can describe much better than I can. I will close with a specific question I asked some of the Minister's constituents in the Province of Quebec when they appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. We have seen the Quebec medical system evolve, and I have worked with people in the system and some of my colleagues have trained in the system. At the Committee hearings I asked this question: "Is the medical care system in Quebec better or worse than the one in Ontario?" The answer is on the records of the Committee, Mr. Speaker; it is worse in Quebec than in Ontario.

That is testimony to the system as it has evolved in the Province of Quebec compared to the way it has evolved in Ontario. That comment was made with obvious regret by the physician who represented a group of physicians from that Province at the Committee.
I again offer my support to those principles of the Bill which I think are important to all Canadians, Mr. Speaker. I shall work with my Party to overcome in the future those problems about which I have expressed general concern.

Start telling the truth.

Mr. Speaker, that was not my comment; that was my question. speechtext: Because of the language or the system?

Because of the system. My colleague is originally from the Caribbean and was the head of surgery at St. Mary's Hospital. He left because of the system which he was doomed to failure because of the way it was being practised in Quebec. That has been emphasized time and again by people within the system. It is not the doctors who suffer, it is the patients. That is what the Minister fails to see, Mr. Speaker. Inevitably, the level of patient care deteriorates because of the lack of ability of those people working within the system to provide the level of care which those patients should have. That is the potential for all of Canada if the Minister continues on in her attitude, and that is too bad.

I would like to make a brief comment, Mr. Speaker. It is difficult to listen to the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) and not get the impression that there is a kind of schizophrenia in the approach of the Conservatives to this Bill. The Bill is designed to create in all provinces of Canada a similarity with the Province of Quebec, as in the Province of Quebec there is no extra billing. On the one hand, how can the Hon. Member try to make the point-
He quoted.

I understand that, but you quote things for a purpose. He quoted the contention of the witness before the committee who said that the health care system in Quebec was worse than in Ontario, presumably because of some characteristic of the health care system in Quebec which distinguishes it from other provinces. One of the few things which does that is that there is no extra billing. Therefore, I ask the Hon. Member how he can on the one hand quote something which indicates that the health care system, which has the very characteristics the Canada Health Act is designed to bring about in all provinces, is in a bad situation, and at the same time indicate that he is going to vote for the Bill? I do not understand how he can say one thing and do another, or perhaps I misunderstand the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose the implication of "schizophrenia" implies there are two possibilities when, indeed, I do not know whether there is any philosophical consistency in any of the approaches of the New Democratic

April 2, 1984
Canada Health Act
Party. What I would like to clarify, first of all, is that I never even mentioned extra billing. What I am talking about is a level of bureaucracy which is trying, from its vantage point, to tell a doctor where he can practise or how he should practise and under what constraints. It is trying to say how the system will work. For instance, as a very specific example, if a consultation were required under the system as it was practised-I do not know if it is the same way now in Quebec- this might mean that a patient could well be exposed to radiation through an entirely new set of x-rays just so an additional consultation could be undertaken on behalf of that patient. That is the only way that a specialist would be able to be considered financially, if you will, for a consultation on behalf of a patient. Those are the types of things which happen.
Those impositions, such as telling a doctor where he can or cannot practise, are every bit as important as anything like extra billing. If the Hon. Member wants to talk about extra billing, I can talk about that as well. However, I suggest to every Hon. If the figure of $3 million was wrong, then I will easily apologize. If the $1.1 million is correct, then that only indicates a level required to support 22 Canadian lives rather than 60. In terms of whether it is the Province of Alberta or any other province, the province has the responsibility to the citizens-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

That is very much the point. The people in my area of Bruce-Grey who are living in a certain environment
and who are involved in activities as Canadians in a province of Canada, have every right to expect to receive health care at levels which are the same, as far as possible, as those in high density downtown urban areas. That is a principle which I fear is jeopardized by the attitude of the Minister because, I believe, the sensitivity, to start with, is certainly not there. It is hard enough at the provincial level to relate to the individual concerns of a small community, let alone try to do that at the federal level, and we are talking about countless communities across Canada. We cannot manage what we are doing here now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a factual question. Could the Hon. Member tell us if, in his riding, the people have unfettered access to general family practice and to specialist services without extra billing? In other words, if someone becomes sick, can that person be admitted to a hospital in his area, and be given anaesthetist services without having to sign forms saying that he realizes there is extra billing involved? Can a woman find an obstetrician and gynaecologist quite easily who offers these services? Are there choices or do people have to drive great distances to find doctors who are opted in? I would like to know the answer to that question, because I have heard that people in rural areas sometimes have limited choices. I wonder if the Hon. Member could give us some background on that?

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the question because I believe it goes right to the heart of the whole issue. I believe the short answer, which I would like to clarify at some other time, is that in the community I personally lived in, yes, indeed, to a level which is beyond most other communities in that area, and that is the second part of the answer. There is no extra billing. I did not extra bill as a physician. In fact, when I started practice we often got paid in kind. So I know where the beef is sometimes. I do not believe that is really what the Hon. Member wanted to ask, with all due respect. There is no extra billing there but there are many physicians who would rather, because of the professional comfort-forgetting for the moment about their personal lives- have the security of working in an area where they have the backup of specialists. Those are things which we are evolving in the smaller communities as much as possible. When we can support the infrastructure which is important in a local hospital, and when the community at large feels that that is something we should work for, we do that. We have been able to do that, but we have done it with some difficulty because we have a bureaucracy which has its own level of control, whether in putting in an operating room, or providing another anaesthetic machine, a capital expenditure program, or whatever it is. At one more level, with the lack of sensitivity which comes when you have to do that, there are increased dangers, Mr. Speaker.

practicing physician. Therefore, would you ask the House for unanimous consent to continue this discussion a little longer.
