speakeroldname: Mr. Al MacBain (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILINGUALISM-MINORITY RIGHTS IN MANITOBA-INQUIRY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF RESOLUTIONS IN PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for the continued interest he is showing for minority language rights across Canada. I would like to assure him that the federal Government is strongly committed to the protection and enhancement of such rights.
In 1870 the Parliament of Canada enacted the Manitoba Act to establish the Province of Manitoba. This Act is part of the constitution of Canada. Special constitutional protection was provided in that Act for the use of the English and French languages in the courts and legislature of Manitoba. In particular it was provided in Section 23 of the Manitoba Act that the Acts of the legislature of Manitoba shall be printed and published in both English and French. However, in 1890 the Manitoba legislature purported to abolish this constitutional protection and its laws were thereafter passed in English only. On December 13 of 1979 the Supreme Court of Canada reaffirmed the constitutional protection under Section 23 of the Manitoba Act in holding that the 1890 law was invalid.
The Hon. Member will also remember that an agreement was reached on May 16, 1983 by the Government of Canada and the Government of Manitoba to modify the Manitoba Act so that the Government and Legislative Assembly of Manitoba could fulfil their constitutional obligations in an orderly way.
The democratically elected Government of Manitoba has made all possible efforts to secure the adoption of the required constitutional resolution. Unfortunately, we are all aware of the political deadlock which led to the prorogation of the Manitoba Legislature.
In light of these events, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has already stated that the federal Government is exploring the avenues that are open to it and that he is discussing the

April 2, 1984
Adjournment Debate
matter with his Ministers. As indicated by the Prime Minister, a serious option is to go before the Supreme Court. I can assure the Hon. Member that this matter is under active consideration and that a decision should be announced very shortly.

subtopic: FISHERIES-GREAT LAKES SPORTS FISHING-IMPORTANCE TO TOURIST INDUSTRY. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
FISHERIES-GREAT LAKES SPORTS FISHING-IMPORTANCE TO TOURIST INDUSTRY. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rose in the House a few days ago to pose a question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) concerning the subject of enhancement of our fisheries resource in the Great Lakes. The Minister is aware, as I am, that this is only part of a larger question, the protection of our environment and conservation of our natural resources.
In my speech today I would like to touch briefly on the broader themes mentioned above and try to relate the enhancement of sports fishing to those themes. The Minister will know that Canada's reputation as a tourist attraction rests with its beautiful scenery, sparkling lakes and its clean air. It is becoming increasingly difficult to protect those resources. The dictates of economics are threatening to overwhelm the careful judgments of environmentalists. For example, the lower Niagara River is indeed a disgrace. This adversely affects the sports fishing which is the topic of my speech today.
We certainly do not wish to develop the reputation in the eyes of potential tourists as a country which is polluting itself to death. It goes without saying that environmental questions are very much linked to the tourism industry. Tourism is the largest single employer in Canada, providing jobs for over one million people in this country. Those jobs are on the line if our clean air and water are lost.
What about the acid rain question? Fish cannot live in water that is acidic. When the fish die a whole chapter of Canadian history dies with them, along with a host of companies which produce the equipment used by fishermen. For example, in Fort Erie, in my riding a fine line of fishing lures are turned out by Williams Gold Ltd. The Minister is aware of the problem, no doubt. He knows that our fisheries are being destroyed by overly acidic lakes and rivers. I would expect that he will make the appropriate representations on behalf of Canadians to ensure that the problem is looked after.
Sports fishing is a subject which deserves, in my opinion, much more attention on the national level. In fact, there are individuals and groups in this country who are lobbying very strongly for more positive ways of enhancing this very important sport, and I say more power to them. I just received a letter today on this very subject. The writer informed me that 95 per cent of the sports fishing stocking is done by the United States states bordering on the Great Lakes.
I am a fisherman myself and believe that there certainly are many ways to go about enhancing our sports fishing industry in this country, thereby indirectly improving our potential for attracting those very elusive tourist dollars which we need in
our country and indeed which seem to be slipping away into the United States because of the higher costs of vacationing in Canada. For example, gasoline is almost double the price here. Therefore, our fishing will have to be pretty good. We must make a concerted effort to publicize the fact that the Great Lakes sports fishery is a resource representing excellent recreational facilities.
With regard to the onshore facilities, provisions must be made to accommodate boats, trailers, and recreational vehicles in areas close to lakes and rivers with good sports fishing potential. Breakwaters must be built to protect marinas and appropriate markings placed for navigation. The onshore facilities are all for nought if a varied and healthy fishery is not present to attract anglers to the improved and expanded facilities which I have described. This should include hatchery facilities and equipment and manpower to undertake comprehensive stocking and restocking of our lakes. The federal Government should work with the provinces to encourage and assist in the restocking which is so imperative. All this takes money, but most of all it takes the political will of committed people at all levels of government.
I will be interested in hearing the response to my question in which I asked the Minister to identify any new programs which would enhance sports fishing on the Great Lakes. I would hope that any new programs would contain the elements I have mentioned. If not, I trust that he would give my suggestions serious thought, given that we are dealing with a resource of tremendous potential, if wisely used.
In conclusion, I call upon the Government to consider seriously means to improve the situation for Canadians and visiting fishermen alike. Briefly, such measures should include monitoring and preserving the quality of our air and water, expansion of facilities to accommodate tourists and tax cuts to ensure that prices are reasonable, and improved conservation and enhancement of our fisheries resources. By actively pursuing these goals, we can improve the quality of life not only for visitors but for those of us who are fortunate enough to live in this beautiful country, to enjoy the outdoors and to enjoy fishing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Harquail (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES-GREAT LAKES SPORTS FISHING-IMPORTANCE TO TOURIST INDUSTRY. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the question of the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz). He has always struck me as being a Member who is sincere about his work. He has not disappointed me at all this evening. Personally, I share his concerns about sports fishing because of its great importance in the Atlantic area, certainly up in the Restigouche area which I have the honour to represent. The mighty Restigouche River and the Atlantic salmon which come up it to spawn and other activities which include sports fishing have been of a personal interest to me for years.
I am delighted to see that the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), is present in the House. I know he supports me in what I will have to say. Hon. Members
April 2, 1984

will know that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) is keenly interested in the total sports fishery questions across Canada. The Minister has been involved in an active dialogue with sports fishermen and recently sponsored a national conference on the subject. The sports fishery is recognized as an important element of the nation's tourist industry and has a great effect upon the economy. The Department is most interested in taking steps to ensure and nurture its growth.
The Department of Fisheries already has in place in Ontario programs of major significance to the sports fishery. Over 400 small craft harbour facilities are operated in Ontario. In Fiscal year 1983-84, over $17 million have been invested in new and improved facilities. The Sea Lamprey Control Program operated out of Sault Ste. Marie is fundamental to the continued existence of the sports fishery in the Great Lakes. Finally, our Great Lakes Research Branch provides much of the information used in identifying fisheries resource problems and developing solutions to them.
Hon. Members will also understand that the nature of the Department's activities in Ontario is different from coastal fisheries, since the responsibility for day to day management of the fishery has been delegated to the province. Thus, there may be considerable interest among members of the sports fishing public in activities similar to our Salmonid Enhancement Program in British Columbia which has been very successful, as is witnessed by the submission to which the Hon. Member referred.
However, the first move along these lines must come from the provinces. We know from past experience in the West Coast Salmonid Enhancement Program that it must continue and go forward. Much has been accomplished in rehabilitating fish stocks with the assistance and co-operation of the public at large. There is an important word in all of these matters facing the fishery today, co-operation. Such involvement has paid big dividends in British Columbia over the past years in terms of the awareness of the resource and support for action to deal with these urgent problems. As a direct consequence, all fisheries, including the sport fishery, will reap significant benefits in the long term. We would be pleased at any time to discuss with the Province of Ontario the very subject that has been raised by the Hon. Member here today, means with which we can move similar initiatives in Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, on December 20 last, I raised a question with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) concerning the very high levels of unemployment in my constituency of Burnaby, B.C. I pointed out to the Prime Minister at that time that the latest figures showed that over
5,000	people were collecting unemployment insurance, and that many more were on welfare, their unemployment insurance having run out.
Adjournment Debate
For the past six months, I have taken the opportunity to canvass door to door in my constituency and listen to the concerns of the people I represent. There is no question, both as a result of that door to door canvass and as a result of mail I have received from my constituents and telephone calls to my constituency office, that by far the most important issue which faces the people of Burnaby at the present time is the question of unemployment, specifically jobs and job security.
I recently spoke at a high school in my riding to a group of about 100 students in Grades 11 and 12. I asked how many of them had a parent or older brother or sister who was presently out of work and looking for a job. Over half the students in that group raised their hands.
This issue is the overwhelming concern of the people I represent, and the response of the prime Minister to that question on December 20 was completely unsatisfactory. The Prime Minister said that we have short-term make-work projects such as Canada Works or Summer Canada Works. My constituents want meaningful permanent jobs. They do not want unemployment insurance, welfare or stop-gap employment. Instead of creating such permanent jobs, this Government's policies in many instances have the opposite effect, and destroy those jobs. For example, grants to assist large corporations in replacing labour with capital will effectively throw people out of work.
Comparatively, Canadians have an incredibly wealthy country. We have rich resources, energy and a skilled labour force. Many people ask what on earth has gone wrong that we cannot put this all together to ensure that we have a full employment economy. Instead, we have been de-industrializing in this nation. The manufacturing sector has shrunk. We are increasingly dependent on our resources as hewers of wood and drawers of water. We continue the madness of exporting unprocessed raw materials. The export of raw logs from British Columbia has increased dramatically. Coal and other raw materials are not being processed in Canada.
We continue to rely very heavily on imports of manufactured goods, mining, agricultural and logging machinery, instead of creating jobs by manufacturing that machinery here in Canada. We continue to ship our goods abroad on foreign bottoms instead of shipping them on Canadian ships. Not only do we have to begin the process of creating a strong and viable manufacturing sector in this country, we have to take a tough look at the structure of work itself.
Just last week a woman told me on her doorstep that she was 54 years old and had a number of friends whose children would love to be working right now but could not find work. She said she had been working for 30 years and would be quite prepared to give up her job as long as she had the security of a proper pension. We must look at creative possibilities for the creation of jobs such as early retirement of full pension, the question of the length of the work week itself and effective retraining programs.

April 2, 1984
Adjournment Debate
There are some who ask how we are going to finance all of those programs. We must effectively declare war on unemployment and make it our number one priority. In the short term, that means capital works projects, putting more money into reforestation, and the acceleration of municipal works projects, energy conservation projects and housing construction. It means putting people to work now. In the longer term, it means reindustrializing and the creation of a manufacturing sector.
The Prime Minister took the commendable initiative of promoting peace worldwide. I suggest that he and his Government now have an obligation to make their number one priority the creation of jobs. The people of Burnaby whom I have the honour to represent are demanding that the Government make meaningful job creation its number one priority. Until then, the Government is effectively condemning literally thousands of people to the economic scrap heap. As the Catholic bishops so eloquently noted in their report of a little over a year ago, that, Mr. Speaker, is fundamentally immoral. My constituents and the people of Canada deserve better.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Dubois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
On behalf of the Minister, Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the question raised by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) on December 20, 1983 concerning measures taken by the Government to offer permanent and worthwhile jobs to Canadians.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I might say that even during this period of financial restraint, the Government has earmarked an unprecedented share of its budget for job creation. Total funds allocated this fiscal year are over $1.2 billion and they will exceed $1.1 billion next year, enabling us to find employment for more than 600,000 Canadians.
The creation of permanent jobs is an objective of the Government, but that cannot be achieved overnight. The Hon. Member has said that young people swell the ranks of the unemployed; unfortunately, it is true that they have a higher unemployment rate because they lack job experience and training. Some employers are reluctant to hire workers without experience, and young people have few opportunities to benefit from on-the-job training.
To put a stop to this vicious circle, the Government has decided to combine its job creation programs so that its human resources initiatives would be united under one or two action strategies, and we now have two programs, Career Access and the Youth Job Corps, which meet this purpose.
The Job Corps, under which each project can be financed for up to three years, offers to those who suffer from any employment handicap the possibility of acquiring basic skills, of getting job counselling and of gaining actual job experience.
The Career Access Program complements the first one by offering employers subsidies so that they may hire people without experience and give them the opportunity to receive on the job training and acquire work experience. While both programs are not specifically aimed at young people, it is expected that they will make up the majority of participants during the next two years.
Two more job-creation programs, Canada Works, and the Local Employment Assistance and Development Program, as well as summer jobs for students will provide our young people with valuable work experience which should increase their employability in the eyes of future employers. During this financial year and the next, we expect that almost 344,000 young people will take advantage of direct job-creation programs.
Mr. Speaker, the government is strongly committed to helping the unemployed find the full-time jobs they deserve. The enormous funds earmarked for direct job creation and training under the Occupational Training Act, the numerous schemes announced in the April budget and the appointment of a Minister of State (Youth), in this case Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette, show that the government is determined to create jobs. I would ask the Hon. Member to advise his electors to go to the Canada Employment Centre and apply to the Career Access program aimed at young people and other groups at a disadvantage on the labour market.
